r: يقف أكثر من ثلاثة ملايين حاج جاءوا من جميع أنحاء العالم على جبل عرفات اليوم الاثنين، ليؤدوا الركن الأعظم في فريضة الحج، ويتجه الحجاج ابتداء من فجر اليوم إلى عرفات ليقضوا نهاره في معية الله بعدما فرغوا من قضاء يوم التروية في مني اقتداء بسنة المصطفي صلي الله عليه وسلم‏ وبعد ساعات من الآن سوف يؤم فضيلة الشيخ جموع الحجاج الموريتانيين في مخيمهم بعرفات في صلاتي الظهر والعصر ويلقي خطبة عرفة التي تتناول عادة مواضيع تهم الحجاج أولا فيما يتعلق بمناسكهم وتتعرض لمختلف التحديات التي تواجه الأمة الإسلامية مع وقفات وعظية وإرشادية

t: Commentary on Nukhbat al-Fikar fi Mustalah Ahl al-Athar — Tape Six, continued
a: شرح نخبة الفكر في مصطلح أهل الأثر الشريط السادس تابع
b:
in the name of god, the most merciful, the compassionate. praise be to god, lord of the worlds, and may god bless our prophet muhammad and grant him peace, and his family and his companions all together. to proceed:

the hafiz (may god have mercy on him) says: "then the impugning of a narrator (ṭaʿn) is either on account of the narrator's lying, or his being suspected of that, or the grossness of his error, or his heedlessness, or his moral transgression (fisq), or his delusion (wahm), or his contradicting [more reliable narrators] (mukhālafah), or his being unknown (jahālah), or his innovation in religion (bidʿah), or his poor memory."

so he has mentioned here these categories among the categories of impugning, according to his own arrangement; and it differs from the arrangement followed by the majority of the specialists in hadith terminology, which is the arrangement we set out earlier. on that arrangement the categories come out fewer than on this division, because in this division some of the items share a single name; so for him to mention them, while they share a name, as separate categories is something that increases the number without much benefit. for that reason we did not adopt this arrangement — but there is no harm in expounding it,
r: بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم الحمد لله رب العالمين، وصلى الله وسلم على نبينا محمد وعلى آله وأصحابه أجمعين، أما بعد فيقول الحافظ رحمه الله: \"ثم الطعن إما أن يكون لكذب الراوي أو تهمته بذلك أو فحش غلطه أو غفلته أو فسقه أو وهمه أو مخالفته أو جهالته أو بدعته أو سوء حفظه\" فذكر هنا هذه الأقسام من أقسام الطعن على حسب ترتيبه هو، وهو يختلف عن الترتيب الذي عليه جمهور أهل المصطلح، وهو الترتيب الذي سقناه سابقا، فتكون الأقسام به أقل من هذا التقسيم، لأن هذا التقسيم بعضه يشترك في الاسم، فذكره مع كونه مشتركا في الاسم كأقسام مما يزيد العدد من غير كبير فائدة، فلذلك لم ننتهج هذا لكن لا بأس بشرحه،

t: The Sheikh Lectures at Several Camps in Mina
a: الشيخ يحاضر في عدة مخيمات في منى
b:
as part of his activities for this year's hajj season, the sheikh delivered several lectures at the camps of mina. he also led the assembled mauritanian pilgrims in the noon and the afternoon prayers, and delivered the arafah sermon. his lectures over these blessed days may be summed up as follows:

1. "the arafah sermon": in it the sheikh surveyed the lessons and the higher purposes to be drawn, by following a number of moments from the pilgrimage of the messenger of god (may god bless him and grant him peace) and what they indicate of the greatness of islam, its tolerance and its comprehensiveness. he closed it by praying that the hajj of every pilgrim be accepted and blameless, and he extended the supplication to the muslims at large. may god reward him with the best of reward and preserve him long as a treasure for islam and the muslims.

2. a lecture entitled "the prophetic guidance on struggling against the self and on standing in prayer by night", which his eminence delivered at the 4shabab camp set up at mina by the 4shabab foundation for purposeful islamic media.

3. a lecture entitled "what the two testimonies of faith require", which the sheikh delivered at the camp of the mauritanian pilgrims. in it the sheikh dwelt on the lessons and the higher purposes that follow from what the two testimonies require — by way of exhortation, of guidance, and of setting out the rulings — and dwelt on the major challenges facing the muslim community.

4. a lecture entitled "the marks of an accepted hajj", which he delivered at the al-mahmal camp in the towers of mina.
r:
ضمن نشاطاته لموسم الحج لهذا العام قدم الشيخ عدة محاضرات في مخيمات منىً، كما أَم جموع الحجاج الموريتانيين في صلاتي الظهر والعصر، وألقى خطبة عرفة ، وتلخصت محاضراته لهذه الأيام المباركة في:

1- "خطبة عرفة": استعرض فيها الشيخ العبر والمقاصد من خلال تتبع وقفات من حجة رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم ودلالاتها في عظمة الإسلام وسماحته وشموليته، وختمها بالدعاء بالقبول والحج المبرور لكل الحجاج، وعمم الدعاء على عامة المسلمين. فجزاه الله خير الجزاء وأدامه ذخرا للإسلام والمسلمين.

2 – محاضرة بعنوان: "هدي النبوة في مجاهدة النفس وقيام الليل"، ألقاها فضيلته في مخيم فور شباب الذي أقامته مؤسسة فور شباب للإعلام الإسلامي الهادف في منىً .

3- محاضرة بعنوان: " مقتضيات الشهادتين"، ألقاها الشيخ في مخيم الحجاج الموريتانيين، وقف فيها الشيخ على العبر والمقاصد من مقتضيات الشهادتين وعظا وإرشادا وتبيانا للأحكام، ووقوفا عند التحديات الكبرى التي تواجه الأمة الإسلامية.

4- محاضرة بعنوان: " علامات الحج المقبول" ألقاها في مخيم المحمل بأبراج منىً.

t: Works and Recordings by the Sheikh to Be Exhibited at the International Book Fair in Riyadh
a: عرض مؤلفات وأشرطة للشيخ في المعرض الدولي للكتاب بالرياض
b:
works and recordings by sheikh muhammad al-hasan al-dedew — may god preserve him — will be exhibited at this year's international book fair in riyadh, which is organised by the cultural affairs sector of the ministry of culture and information during the month of rabi al-awwal 1432 ah.

mu'assasat al-ummah for publishing and distribution in riyadh will have sole charge of exhibiting these works and recordings at its own stand at the international fair. the sheikh's exhibited items consist of two new books: nathr al-ifādāt ʿalā matn al-waraqāt, which is a commentary on the text of the book al-waraqāt of imam al-haramayn; and al-nahr al-ʿadhb, which is the second release in this series and comprises six lectures on governance in accordance with the sharia (al-siyāsah al-sharʿiyyah). the foundation will also exhibit an album in the form of an audio disc containing the second part of the programme "mafāhīm", which hosts the sheikh on "4shabab channel" throughout the days of the month of ramadan.
r:
ستعرض مؤلفات وأشرطة للشيخ محمد الحسن الددو - حفظه الله - في معرض الكتاب الدولي لهذا العام في الرياض، الذي ينظمه قطاع الشؤون الثقافية بوزارة الثقافة والإعلام خلال شهر ربيع الأول 1432هـ.

مؤسسة الأمة للنشر والتوزيع بالرياض ستنفرد بعرض هذه المؤلفات والأشرطة في جناحها الخاص بالمعرض الدولي، وتتمثل معروضات الشيخ في كتابين جديدين هما: كتاب: " نثر الإفادات على متن الورقات"؛ وهو شرح لمتن كتاب " ورقات إمام الحرمين". وكتاب: " النهر العذب"؛وهو الإصدار الثاني من هذه السلسلة، ويضم ست محاضرات حول السياسة الشرعية.كما ستعرض المؤسسة كذلك ألبوم على شكل قرص مسموع يحتوي على الجزء الثاني من برنامج "مفاهيم" الذي يستضيف الشيخ على "قناة فور شباب" طيلة أيام شهر رمضان.

t: Commentary on al-Jazariyyah — Part One
a: شرح الجزرية الجزء الأول
b:
in the name of god, the most merciful, the compassionate. praise be to god, lord of the worlds. i invoke blessings and peace upon him who was sent as a mercy to the worlds, and upon his family and his companions and whoever has taken his guidance for guidance and his sunnah for a way, until the day of judgement. peace be upon you, and the mercy of god and his blessings.

to proceed: god, be he exalted, sent the qur'an down upon muhammad (peace and blessings be upon him) in a clear arabic tongue. gabriel (peace be upon him) brought it to the messenger of god (peace and blessings be upon him) in instalments over twenty-three years, coming down according to events and according to what the people of the earth asked about. that was a channel of contact between the people of heaven and the people of the earth, and a bond between the creation and the creator — mighty and exalted is he — by the setting out of what he wants from them and the legislating of what he is content with for them. god sealed the messages to the people of the earth with the message of muhammad (peace and blessings be upon him), and sealed the books sent down to the people of the earth with the qur'an; and he made it confirming the truth that was before it, a guardian over all the books, and abrogating them. so god accepts from no one, after the descent of the qur'an, any religion but this islam which this qur'an contains. it was sent down in a variety of modes: among them, that the angel would come in the form of a man and speak to the messenger of god (peace and blessings be upon him), and he would retain from him what he said,
r: بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم الحمد لله رب العالمين وأصلي وأسلم على من بعث رحمة للعالمين وعلى آله وأصحابه ومن اهتدى بهديه واستن بسنته إلى يوم الدين، السلام عليكم ورحمة الله وبركاته، أما بعد فإن الله تعالى أنزل القرآن على محمد (ص) بلسان عربي مبين، وقد جاء به جبريل عليه السلام إلى رسول الله (ص) منجما في ثلاث وعشرين سنة، ينزل بحسب الوقائع وبحسب ما يسأل عنه أهل الأرض وكان ذلك اتصالا بين أهل السماء وأهل الأرض، وارتباطا بين الخلق والخالق، جل وعلا ببيان ما يريده منهم وتشريع ما يرتضيه لهم، وقد ختم الله الرسائل إلى أهل الأرض برسالة محمد (ص)، وختم الكتب المنزلة إلى أهل الأرض بالقرآن، وجعله مصدقا لما بين يديه من الحق ومهيمنا على كل الكتب وناسخا لها، فلا يقبل الله من أحد بعد نزول القرآن دينا إلا هذا الإسلام الذي تضمنه هذا القرآن، وقد أنزل على هيآت متنوعة، فمنها أن يأتي الملك على هيئة رجل فيكلم رسول الله (ص) فيعي عنه ما يقول،

t: Commentary on al-Jazariyyah — Part Two
a: شرح الجزرية الجزء الثاني
b: and by this you know that hafs al-duri, for example, died in the third century, and al-khaqani died in the fourth century, and makki ibn abi talib died in the fifth century. the people of al-andalus in general were renowned for their mastery of this science, and for that reason makki was a renewer in it. then after him came abu amr al-dani, who is without dispute the foremost authority in all the sciences of the qur'an; and after him his student abu dawud sulayman ibn al-najih, who was likewise al-dani's successor in this science. the people of al-andalus were renowned for the sciences of the rules of qur'anic recitation (tajwīd), and for qur'anic exegesis (tafsīr) as well — among them ibn atiyyah, ibn juzayy, al-qurtubi, abu bakr ibn al-arabi and others — and for others among the leading authorities in tajwid, such as abu hayyan and ibn al-faras al-maliki, the author of the book ahkam al-qur'an. they have a very great many works in the service of the qur'an.
r: وبهذا تعلمون أن حفص الدوري مثلا توفي في القرن الثالث والخاقاني توفي في القرن الرابع، ومكي بن أبي طالب توفي في القرن الخامس، وأهل الأندلس عموما اشتهروا بإتقان هذا العلم ولذلك فإن مكيا كان مجددا فيه ثم جاء بعده أبو عمرو الداني وهو إمام علوم القرآن كلها بلا منازع، ثم بعده تلميذه أبو داود سليمان بن النجيح وهو كذلك خليفة الداني في هذا العلم، فأهل الأندلس اشتهروا بعلوم التجويد وبتفسير القرآن كذلك فمنهم ابن عطية وابن جزي والقرطبي وأبو بكر بن العربي وغيرهم من أئمة أهل التجويد كأبي حيان وابن الفرس المالكي مؤلف كتاب أحكام القرآن، فلهم مؤلفات كثيرة جدا في خدمة القرآن.

t: Commentary on al-Jazariyyah — The Last Tape
a: شرح الجزرية الشريط الأخير
b:
i shall repeat the text of the previous chapter in order to correct the errors in it. the author (may god have mercy on him) said:

*and know what is written separated (maqṭūʿ) and what is written joined (mawṣūl), and the written tāʾ, in the muṣḥaf of the imam, in what has come down in it.*

*so write separately in ten words: an lā — together with maljaʾin, and lā ilāha illā,*

*and taʿbudū [in] yā sīn, the second [instance in] hūd; lā yushrikna, tushrik, yadkhulanna, taʿlū ʿalā,*

*allā yaqūlū, lā aqūla, immā — in al-raʿd; and the one with the fatḥah, write joined; and ʿammā*

*nuhū: write [these] separately. mimmā in al-rūm and al-nisāʾ, with a difference of opinion in al-munāfiqūn; am man assasa,*

*fuṣṣilat, al-nisāʾ and al-dhabḥ, ḥaythumā; and an lam with the fatḥah; the kasrah of innamā*

*in al-anʿām; and the one with the fatḥah, yadʿūna, both [instances]; and a difference of opinion has occurred in al-anfāl and al-naḥl;*

*and every kulla mā; saʾaltumūhu, and there is disagreement over it; raddū; likewise qul biʾsamā; and set out the cases of writing joined:*

*khalaftumūnī and ishtarū; in fī mā write separately; awḥiya, afaḍtum, ishtahat, yablū, both [instances],*

*the second faʿalna, and waqaʿa [in] al-rūm, kullā; tanzīl, [al-]ẓullah — and write the rest of them joined.*

*fa-aynamā, as in al-naḥl, write joined; and it differs in al-shuʿarāʾ, al-aḥzāb and al-nisāʾ — so set that out.*

*and write joined fa-illam [in] hūd, an lan najʿala, najmaʿa, kay lā taḥzanū, taʾsaw, ʿalā*

*ḥajj, ʿalayka ḥaraj; and their writing separately of ʿan man yashāʾu, man tawallā, yawmahum*

*and mā li-hādhā, wa-lladhīna hāʾulāʾ, taḥīna — in the [muṣḥaf of the] imam write joined; and wahala*

*and wazanūhum and kālūhum — write joined; likewise min al-, and hā and yā: do not separate them.*
r:
سأعيد متن الباب السابق لتصحيح الأخطاء التي فيه، قال المؤلف رحمه الله:

واعْرِفْ لمقطوع وموصول وتا** في مصحف الإمام فيما قد أتى

فاقطع بعشر كلمات ألا** معْ مَلْجَإٍ ولا إله إلا

وتعبدوا يَاسِينَ ثاني هودَ لا** يشركن تشركْ يدخُلَنْ تعلوا على

ألَّا يقولوا لا أقولٍَ إما** بالرعد والمفتوح صل وعما

نهوا اقطعوا مما بروم والنسا** خلف المنافقين أمَّن أسسا

فصلت النسا وذبح حيثما** وأن لم المفتوح كسر إنما

الانعام والمفتوح يدعون معا** وخلف الانفال ونحل وقعا

وكل ما سألتموه واختلف** ردوا كذا قل بيسما والوصل صف

خلفتموني واشتروا في ما اقطعا** أوحي أفضتم اشتهت يبلو معا

ثاني فعلن وقعد روم كلا** تنزيل ظلة وغيرها صلا

فأينما كالنحل صل ومختلف** في الشعرا الأحزاب والنسا وصف

وصل فإلم هود أن لن نجعلا** نجمع كي لا تحزنوا تأسوا على

حج عليك حرج وقطعهم** عن من يشاء من تولى يومهم

ومال هذا والذين هؤلا** تحين في الإمام صل ووهلا

ووزنوهم وكالوهم صل** كذا من ال وها ويا لا تفصل

t: Commentary on al-Jazariyyah — Tape Nine
a: شرح الجزرية الشريط التاسع
b:
in the name of god, the most merciful, the compassionate. praise be to god, lord of the worlds. i invoke blessings and peace upon him who was sent as a mercy to the worlds, and upon his family and his companions and whoever has taken his guidance for guidance and his sunnah for a way, until the day of judgement.

the author (may god, be he exalted, have mercy on him) says: "chapter on the knowledge of the pauses." he set up this chapter to expound an important matter among the matters of qur'anic recitation (tajwīd), namely the ruling on pausing and on beginning again. pausing (waqf), in the language, is the verbal noun of waqafa, which is used both intransitively and transitively. one says "so-and-so waqafa in the prayer", meaning that he stood; and one says "so-and-so waqafa his mount or his she-camel", when he brought it to a halt. and from this is the saying of antarah
r: بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم الحمد لله رب العالمين وأصلي وأسلم على من بعث رحمة للعالمين وعلى آله وأصحابه ومن اهتدى بهديه واستن بسنته إلى يوم الدين يقول المؤلف رحمه الله تعالى: باب معرفة الوقوف عقد هذا الباب لبيان أمر مهم من أمور التجويد وهو حكم الوقف والابتداء، والوقف في اللغة مصدر وقف تستعمل لازمة وتستعمل متعدية، فيقال وقف فلان في الصلاة أي قام، ويقال وقف فلان راحلته أو ناقته إذا حبسها، ومنه قول عنترة

t: Commentary on al-Jazariyyah — Tape Three
a: شرح الجزرية الشريط الثالث
b:
in the name of god, the most merciful, the compassionate. praise be to god, lord of the worlds. i invoke blessings and peace upon him who was sent as a mercy to the worlds, and upon his family and his companions and whoever has taken his guidance for guidance and his sunnah for a way, until the day of judgement.

to proceed: the author (may god have mercy on him) says: "chapter on the points of articulation of the letters." a bāb, in the language, is a gap in a barrier by which one passes from inside to outside and the reverse — literally so in buildings, as with the door of a house, and by extension in meanings, as with the "chapter" on the points of articulation of the letters. in technical usage it is a name for a group of topics within a discipline which share certain rulings and are marked off from others; and it is set up for whatever stands in need of exposition within the science. now this science, which is the science of qur'anic delivery, has among its topics ones that require a chapter on the points of articulation of the letters to be set up. the letters have already been defined, and they are examined from four aspects. the first aspect: the point of articulation (the point of articulation of the letter). the second aspect: the quality by which the letter is characterised,
r:
بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم الحمد لله رب العالمين وأصلي وأسلم على من بعث رحمة للعالمين وعلى آله وأصحابه ومن اهتدى بهديه واستن بسنته إلى يوم الدين.

أما بعد فيقول المؤلف رحمه الله: باب مخارج الحروف الباب في اللغة فرجة في ساتر يتوصل بها من داخل إلى خارج وبالعكس حقيقةً في المباني كباب الدار وحكما في المعاني كباب مخارج الحروف، وهو في الاصطلاح اسم لطائفة من الفن تشترك في بعض الأحكام وتتميز عن غيرها، وهو يعقد لما يحتاج لبيانه من العلم، فهذا العلم الذي هو علم الأداء من مسائله التي تحتاج إلى عقد باب مخارج الحروف، والحروف قد سبق تعريفها وهي يبٍحث فيها من أربعة أوجه، الوجه الأول: المخرج (مخرج الحرف)، والوجه الثاني الصفة التي يتصف بها الحرف،

t: Commentary on al-Jazariyyah — Tape Eight
a: شرح الجزرية الشريط الثامن
b:
praise be to god, lord of the worlds, and may god bless our prophet muhammad and grant him peace, and his family and his companions and whoever has taken his guidance for guidance and his sunnah for a way, until the day of judgement. peace be upon you, and the mercy of god and his blessings.

to proceed: among the letters there are some that have rulings peculiar to them, so they must be attended to in order that those rulings peculiar to them may be attended to. these letters are the mīm, the nūn and the lām: these three letters depart from the general rules of the letters on account of certain properties peculiar to them, and so there was a need to set out rulings peculiar to them. the author (may god, be he exalted, have mercy on him) set up this chapter to set out the rulings of the mīm and to set out the ruling of the doubled nūn. he said:
r:
الحمد لله رب العالمين وصلى الله وسلم على نبينا محمد وعلى آله وأصحابه ومن اهتدى بهديه واستن بسنته إلى يوم الدين، السلام عليكم ورحمة الله وبركاته.

أما بعد فإن من الحروف ما هو مختص ببعض الأحكام، فلا بد من العناية به للعناية بتلك الأحكام التي تختص به، وهذه الحروف هي الميم والنون واللام فهذه الحروف الثلاثة تخرج عن قواعد الحروف لبعض الاختصاصات التي تختص بها، فاحتيج لبيان أحكام تختص بها، وقد عقد المؤلف رحمه الله تعالى هذا الباب لبيان أحكام الميم ولبيان حكم النون المشددة فقال:

t: Commentary on al-Jazariyyah — Tape Five
a: شرح الجزرية الشريط الخامس
b:
in the name of god, the most merciful, the compassionate. praise be to god, lord of the worlds. i invoke blessings and peace upon him who was sent as a mercy to the worlds, and upon his family and his companions and whoever has taken his guidance for guidance and his sunnah for a way, until the day of judgement. peace be upon you, and the mercy of god, be he exalted, and his blessings.

to proceed: it has already been established that the locations of the points of articulation are five — the cavity, the throat, the tongue, the two lips and the nasal passage. these are five locations, and they are the places where pressure is applied to the air issuing from the lung; and at every place where it is pressed, one of the points of articulation of the letters is formed. it has also already been established that the scholars differed over the number of the points of articulation of the letters, into four positions. the first position is that of al-khalil ibn ahmad al-farahidi, that they are seventeen, and this is what ibn al-jazari chose. the second position is that they are twenty-nine, that is, that every letter has a point of articulation of its own
r: بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم الحمد لله رب العالمين، وأصلي وأسلم على من بعث رحمة للعالمين، وعلى آله وأصحابه ومن اهتدى بهديه واستن بسنته إلى يوم الدين، السلام عليكم ورحمة الله تعالى وبركاته، أما بعد فقد سبق أن مواضع المخارج خمسة، الجوف والحلق واللسان والشفتان والخيشوم، فهذه خمسة مواضع هي محال الضغط على الهواء المنطلق من الرئة، وفي كل مكان ضغط عليه يتركب مخرج من مخارج الحروف، وقد سبق أن العلماء اختلفوا في عدد مخارج الحروف إلى أربعة أقوال: القول الأول قول الخليل بن أحمد الفراهيدي أنها سبعة عشر، وهو اختيار ابن الجزري، القول الثاني أنها تسعة وعشرين أي أن لكل حرف مخرجا

t: Commentary on al-Jazariyyah — Tape Four
a: شرح الجزرية الشريط الرابع
b:
then he said: "chapter on the qualities." he set up this chapter for the qualities of the letters. a quality (ṣifah), in origin, is a descriptive attribute, and whatever distinguishes a thing from something else. qualities are, in origin, of three kinds: essential qualities, accidental qualities, and juridically assigned qualities.

the essential qualities are those upon which god created the thing — such as a person's tallness or shortness, his beauty or ugliness, his whiteness or blackness, and the like; this is an essential quality in him.

the accidental qualities are such as the volitional or active qualities — like motion and rest in a person, and speech and silence; this is an accidental quality, that is, one that comes upon the person.

the third kind is the juridically assigned qualities, and they are the rulings that the lawgiver has attached to the thing — such as ritual purity (ṭahārah) and substantive impurity (najāsah). that this thing is pure, and that it is impure, is not part of how it was created, nor is it something accidental in it; rather it is a ruling that the lawgiver has ordered upon it. this is so in the view of the majority of the people of knowledge, as against the hanafis: for the hanafis hold that the juridically assigned qualities are among the original qualities and not among the accidental ones. so they make the rulings foundational, holding that the lawgiver is disclosing what was already there in the original constitution of the thing; and thus they hold that the original state of water is purity, so that this is an original quality of it, and that the original state of urine is impurity, so that this is an original quality of it,
r: ثم قال: باب الصفات عقد هذا الباب لصفات الحروف، والصفة في الأصل النعت وما يميز الشيء عن غيره، والصفات ثلاثة أقسام في الأصل، صفات ذاتية، وصفات عرضية، وصفات حكمية، فالصفات الذاتية هي ما خلق الله عليه الشيء كطول الإنسان وقصره وحسنه وقبحه وبياضه وسواده ونحو ذلك هذه صفة ذاتية فيه، والصفات العرضية كالصفات الاختيارية أو الفعلية كالحركة والسكون في الإنسان، والكلام والسكوت، هذا صفة عرضية أي تعرض للإنسان، والقسم الثالث الصفات الحكمية وهي: ما ناطه الشارع به من الأحكام، كالطهارة والنجاسة، كون هذا الشيء طاهرا وكونه نجسا هذا ليس من خلقته، ولا هو عارض فيه بل هو حكم رتبه الشارع عليه، وهذا عند جمهور أهل العلم خلافا للحنفية فالحنفية يرون أن الصفات الحكمية من الصفات الأصلية لا من الصفات العارضة، فيجعلون الأحكام أصولا يرون أن الشارع كاشف لما كان سابقا في أصل الخلقة، فيرون أن الأصل في الماء الطهارة فهو صفة أصلية له، وأن الأصل في البول النجاسة فهو صفة أصلية له،

t: Commentary on al-Jazariyyah — Tape Seven
a: شرح الجزرية الشريط السابع
b:
in the name of god, the most merciful, the compassionate. praise be to god, lord of the worlds. i invoke blessings and peace upon him who was sent as a mercy to the worlds, and upon his family and his companions and whoever has taken his guidance for guidance and his sunnah for a way, until the day of judgement. peace be upon you, and the mercy of god and his blessings.

the author (may god have mercy on him) says: "chapter on the rāʾs." he set up this chapter for an accidental quality, namely the thinning of the sound that characterises the rāʾ. it has already been established that thickening is a quality of all the elevated letters and that thinning is a quality of all the lowered letters, and that thickening occurs accidentally in three of the lowered letters, namely the rāʾ, the lām and the alif. these three letters are lowered, and yet thickening occurs in them accidentally. since this thickening was an accidental quality, we did not mention it [earlier]. the author (may god, be he exalted, have mercy on him) mentioned what pertains to the rāʾs, then mentioned what pertains to the lāms and the alifs that go with them; and he began with the rāʾs, saying:
r:
بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم الحمد لله رب العالمين وأصلي وأسلم على من بعث رحمة للعالمين، وعلى آله وأصحابه ومن اهتدى بهديه واستن بسنته إلى يوم الدين، السلام عليكم ورحمة الله وبركاته،

يقول المؤلف رحمه الله: باب الراءات عقد هذا الباب لصفة عارضة وهي الترقيق الذي تتصف به الراء، فقد سبق أن التغليظ صفة لكل الحروف المستعلية وأن الترقيق صفة لكل الحروف المستفلة وأن التغليظ يعرض في ثلاثة من الحروف المستفلة وهي الراء واللام والألف، فهذه الحروف الثلاثة مستفلة ومع ذلك يعرض فيها التغليظ، وهذا التغليظ لما كان صفة عارضة لم نذكره، والمؤلف رحمه الله تعالى ذكر ما يتعلق بالراءت ثم ذكر ما يتعلق باللامات والألفات التي معها فبدأ بالراءات فقال:

t: Commentary on al-Jazariyyah — Tape Ten
a: شرح الجزرية الشريط العاشر
b:
in the name of god, the most merciful, the compassionate. praise be to god, lord of the worlds. i invoke blessings and peace upon him who was sent as a mercy to the worlds, and upon his family and his companions and whoever has taken his guidance for guidance and his sunnah for a way, until the day of judgement. peace be upon you, and the mercy of god and his blessings.

the author (may god have mercy on him) says: "chapter on the rāʾs." he set up this chapter for an accidental quality, namely the thinning of the sound that characterises the rāʾ. it has already been established that thickening is a quality of all the elevated letters and that thinning is a quality of all the lowered letters, and that thickening occurs accidentally in three of the lowered letters, namely the rāʾ, the lām and the alif. these three letters are lowered, and yet thickening occurs in them accidentally. since this thickening was an accidental quality, we did not mention it [earlier]. the author (may god, be he exalted, have mercy on him) mentioned what pertains to the rāʾs, then mentioned what pertains to the lāms and the alifs that go with them; and he began with the rāʾs, saying:
r:
بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم الحمد لله رب العالمين وأصلي وأسلم على من بعث رحمة للعالمين، وعلى آله وأصحابه ومن اهتدى بهديه واستن بسنته إلى يوم الدين، السلام عليكم ورحمة الله وبركاته،

يقول المؤلف رحمه الله: باب الراءات عقد هذا الباب لصفة عارضة وهي الترقيق الذي تتصف به الراء، فقد سبق أن التغليظ صفة لكل الحروف المستعلية وأن الترقيق صفة لكل الحروف المستفلة وأن التغليظ يعرض في ثلاثة من الحروف المستفلة وهي الراء واللام والألف، فهذه الحروف الثلاثة مستفلة ومع ذلك يعرض فيها التغليظ، وهذا التغليظ لما كان صفة عارضة لم نذكره، والمؤلف رحمه الله تعالى ذكر ما يتعلق بالراءت ثم ذكر ما يتعلق باللامات والألفات التي معها فبدأ بالراءات فقال:

t: Commentary on al-Jazariyyah — Tape Six
a: شرح الجزرية الشريط السادس
b:
he defined the rules of qur'anic recitation (tajwīd) with a definition that falls short, saying:

*and it is the giving to the letters of their due, of the quality belonging to them, and of what they merit.*

he said that tajwid, in technical usage, is the giving to the letters of their due; and the due of the letters is their necessary qualities, their original qualities, which are these eighteen qualities — this is the letters' due. and "what they merit", in technical usage, is the accidental qualities: the accidental qualities, some of which we have mentioned without covering them exhaustively, such as nasalisation, thinning, thickening and so on. these qualities are called the accidental qualities. so this is a technical usage; otherwise there is no difference in the language between "a due" and "what is merited", because a due is something merited, which the one entitled to it merits. he said:

*and it is the giving to the letters of their due, of the quality belonging to them, and of what they merit.*

وهو إعطاء الحروف حقها** من صفة لها ومستحقها

t: The Islamic Religious Sciences — Tape One
a: العلوم الشرعية -الشريط الأول-
b:
in the name of god, the merciful, the compassionate.

praise belongs to god, lord of the worlds, and may god bless our prophet muhammad and his family and all his companions and grant them peace.

to proceed: god, glorified and exalted, is the all-knowing, the all-aware, and all knowledge is from him, and he knows best. he sent the messengers, upon them be blessing and peace, to people so as to teach them what they need of what sets right their religion and their worldly life, and he sent down upon them the books containing what people need of knowledge. and this that was sent down to people amounts to only a little of his knowledge, glorified and exalted. that is why he said in his address to people: {and you have not been given of knowledge except a little} (sūrat al-isrāʾ 17:85). for all the abundance of what has been sent down of knowledge, and its ramifications, and people's amassing of it and their expansion in it, it neither equals nor diminishes anything of the knowledge of god, glorified and exalted. and this knowledge which he sent down he did not send down to be an arena of rivalry and competition among people, nor to be something by which the pretentious make pretensions and the boastful boast; nor did he send it down to be a way of whiling away time and occupying souls. he sent it down only to be acted upon. so every science upon which no action follows — the basic principle is that there is no benefit in it, and the man of sense ought not to occupy himself with it, because life is short and a person's time is too precious to waste on what is not accompanied by action. for what is weighed on the day of resurrection is deeds, not sciences: the balance on the day of resurrection has placed in it only deeds, whether righteous or evil, weighed by the measures of an atom's weight. and when people see that, that day on which the deeds are weighed makes children grey-haired. they see only the weighing of deeds by the measures of an atom: {so whoever does an atom's weight of good shall see it, and whoever does an atom's weight of evil shall see it} (sūrat al-zalzalah 99:7–8).

god, glorified and exalted, has raised the rank of this knowledge and made it a cause of elevation in this world and the hereafter. therefore the rank of the people of learning with god, glorified and exalted, is high. he called them to witness to the greatest testimony, after he himself had borne witness to it and had made his angels bear witness to it, and said, exalted is he: {god bears witness that there is no god but he, and the angels, and those possessed of knowledge} (sūrat āl ʿimrān 3:18). and he informed us that they alone fear him with the fear that is his due, and said, exalted is he: "only those of his servants who have knowledge fear god" (sūrat fāṭir 35:28). and he gave judgement in their favour over others in his words: {say: are those who know and those who do not know equal? only those of understanding take heed} (sūrat al-zumar 39:9). and he informed us that they alone are qualified to receive from him and to understand his speech, and said, exalted is he: {and these similitudes we strike for people, but none understand them except those who know} (sūrat al-ʿankabūt 29:43). and he informed us that he raises them in degrees in this world and the hereafter, and said, exalted is he: {o you who believe, when it is said to you: make room in the assemblies, then make room; god will make room for you. and when it is said: rise up, then rise up; god will raise those of you who believe and those who have been given knowledge in degrees} (sūrat al-mujādalah 58:11).

the messenger, may god bless him and grant him peace, drew attention to their standing. it is established from him, may god bless him and grant him peace, that he said: "the scholars are the heirs of the prophets." and it is established from him that he said: "whoever god wills good for, he gives him understanding in the religion." and it is established from him, in the hadith of ʿuthman in ṣaḥīḥ al-bukhārī, that he said: "the best of you is he who learns the qur'an and teaches it." likewise he struck a similitude for the learner who teaches, and for the learner who is unable to teach, and for the one who turns away, in what al-bukhari brought out from the hadith of abu musa: "the likeness of what god has sent me with of guidance and knowledge is the likeness of abundant rain that fell upon a land …". and he made clear, may god bless him and grant him peace, that this knowledge is attained only by learning, in what al-bukhari brought out from him in suspended form and ibn abi ʿasim connected in the book al-sunnah, that the prophet, may god bless him and grant him peace, said: "knowledge comes only by learning, and forbearance only by cultivating forbearance."

he made clear, may god bless him and grant him peace, that god chooses for this knowledge a people from among the people of every age. they are his witnesses, who bear witness over the people of their age, and they are his upright ones who carry his revelation. god would not put his revelation in a place of abasement. this revelation is the choicest thing on this earth, and god would not choose over it trustees who are people of negligence, unfit for this level; rather he chooses the best of people for this revelation, which is the best thing in the earth. and whomever god has chosen to be among his trustees over his revelation, he has honoured with a mighty honour. that is why al-bukhari related from some of the predecessors that they used to say: it is not fitting for one who has something of this knowledge with him that he should waste himself. what is meant by wasting himself is several things. among them: that he should not act upon his knowledge, because that is waste in this world and the hereafter. among them: that he should abase himself before others or be a servant to them, so that this strips him of his standing and his learning. and among them likewise: that he should withdraw from people and abandon the teaching of the knowledge with which he has been entrusted, because that is a wasting of himself and of the knowledge he has.

as for god's trust, glorified and exalted, he has taken the covenant and the pledge from whomever he has entrusted with it, that he shall convey what he has been entrusted with; and he mentioned a severe warning against whoever does not do so: {when god took the covenant of those who were given the book: you shall make it clear to people and not conceal it} (sūrat āl ʿimrān 3:187). the prophet, may god bless him and grant him peace, made that clear in his words: "whoever conceals knowledge will be bridled on the day of resurrection with a bridle of fire." and the messenger of god, may god bless him and grant him peace, urged its conveying: it is established from him in the two ṣaḥīḥs that he said: "convey from me, even a single verse; and relate from the children of israel, and there is no harm in it." and it is established from him, may god bless him and grant him peace, likewise that he said: "let the one present among you convey to the one absent, for many a one to whom it is conveyed is more retentive than one who hears it." and it is established from him, may god bless him and grant him peace — in what the authors of the sunan brought out from ibn masʿud, and al-suyuti and others counted among the mass-transmitted hadiths — that he, may god bless him and grant him peace, said: "may god give radiance to a man who hears my words and grasps them and conveys them as he heard them; for many a bearer of understanding is not himself a person of understanding, and many a bearer of understanding conveys it to one who has more understanding than he."

whoever is able to join this caravan and to travel this road and does not do so is the most losing of people in his bargain, because he was given access to the best thing in the earth and occupied himself with what is beneath it — and god most high has said: {would you exchange what is lower for what is better?} (sūrat al-baqarah 2:61). for the best thing in the earth is this revelation sent down from god; and whoever was able to be one of its people and one of god's trustees over it and then fell short in that has lost his bargain. therefore it makes one independent of everything else, while nothing else makes one independent of it. whoever occupies himself with gathering knowledge and serving it, god has guaranteed him what suffices him in this world; for it has come in the hadith that god has guaranteed the provision of the seeker of knowledge. and it is likewise an act of worship of god, even if a person does not act upon it, when he intends to act upon it and preserves it for people. that is why abu ʿabd allah malik ibn anas was asked about one brought forward for execution, of whose life there remains but an hour, as to what act of worship he should spend it in; and he said: a science he learns. it was said: abu ʿabd allah, he will not act upon it. he said: learning it is better than acting upon it. and the imam abu ʿabd allah al-shafiʿi, may god have mercy on him, said: seeking knowledge is better than voluntary prayer. he held that the occupation of those who occupy themselves with knowledge is better than the occupation of those who stand in prayer the whole night. that is why al-suyuti, may god most high have mercy on him, said in al-kawkab al-sāṭiʿ:

*and knowledge is better than a voluntary prayer, for god has already nourished its guarantor with provision.*

al-bayhaqi brought out in the sunan, and abu ʿumar ibn ʿabd al-barr in the introduction to al-tamhīd, and al-hafiz al-baghdadi in sharaf aṣḥāb al-ḥadīth by eleven routes — and he mentioned from the imam ahmad that he declared it sound — from the hadith of ibn masʿud, that the messenger of god, may god bless him and grant him peace, said: "this knowledge will be carried by the upright of every generation, who will repel from it the distortion of the extremists, the false claims of the falsifiers, and the misinterpretation of the ignorant."

but this knowledge, whose distinction and nobility we have mentioned — not everyone who occupies himself with it, or attains some of it, attains this rank and this nobility. that requires a method and a way that is balanced, in which a person balances between knowledge and action, and balances likewise between the kinds of sciences and their objectives and their means, and balances likewise between the results he aims at and the effort he expends. for balance is required by the sharia in all matters, and moderation is required in them. extremism in knowledge — in that a person has no aim and no concern but occupying himself with chasing the stray oddities and rarities of learning — this makes a person unbalanced, and he must be afflicted with extremism; and whoever is afflicted with extremism has followed a step among the steps of satan, and god most high has said: {o you who believe, do not follow the steps of satan} (sūrat al-baqarah 2:208). likewise whoever turns away from this knowledge, or considers something else better than it — such as one who occupies himself with the call to islam at the expense of knowledge and neglects knowledge entirely, or occupies himself with amassing wealth at the expense of knowledge and contents himself with the very least of it — this man too has negligence in him, and negligence too is among the steps of satan, and it is the opposite of the excess just mentioned. likewise whoever occupies himself with one single science and concentrates all his attention on that science will be afflicted with excess in it and negligence in what is besides it, and will lose balance — because knowledge is all of it from god, and part of it completes and perfects another part. for this reason the crime of the curricula in this age of ours against knowledge is by the specialisations, which have made a person study a single particular and go deep in it and neglect what is besides it, so that he is dull in the other matters which are among the conditions for producing the very thing he is occupied with; and if he does not bring the condition, he cannot bring the conditioned.

likewise, among what must be warned against in this field is that many people do not take up for knowledge its instruments and conditions: a man wants to be a scholar and to leap over the distances, and travels for that roads that do not lead to it. knowledge requires, in order to be reached — as the people of learning have it — seven conditions.

the first of them is "going abroad" for it. what is meant by that is that a person should set himself apart for knowledge and not be occupied with managing the affairs of household and livelihood. for one who is among his own people will be occupied with their concerns and will find for himself a standing and a lordship that prevent him from receiving. that is why ʿumar ibn al-khattab said, as al-bukhari brought out from him in the ṣaḥīḥ: "learn before you become lords." for the one who is a lord in his own place cannot humble himself before knowledge. therefore a person must set himself apart from his own people in order to attain this knowledge. the root of that is that god, glorified and exalted, related to us the story of moses in his seeking of knowledge, when he went to al-khidr; and he mentioned that he did not attain this knowledge until he said: "until i reach the junction of the two seas, or i shall journey on for a long time" (sūrat al-kahf 18:60). so he went out from his leadership of the children of israel and his command over them in order to gather this knowledge. and likewise our prophet, may god bless him and grant him peace, did not attain this knowledge until solitude was made beloved to him, so that he would withdraw into the cave of hiraʾ and devote himself there — and that is worship — for a number of nights, and then return to khadijah and take provision for the like of it, until the truth came to him and the angel came to him while he was in the cave of hiraʾ.

this first condition, "the going abroad", can be realised in our age either by an actual going abroad or by a going abroad in feeling. the actual going abroad is that a person should find a time which he cuts out and steals away from his family and his work, in which he sets himself apart and goes out from his place — as in this going out of ours. now this, firstly, from the devotional side, contains a going out to god, glorified and exalted, and a leaving behind our backs of what has been bestowed on us, and a reminder of that going out to him at death, when his caller calls with what is greater than that, at the gathering and the presentation before him, glorified and exalted. and likewise the correcting of the intention at home; and the pebbles and the sand and the atoms of oxygen a person passes by are all written in the balance of his good deeds if he makes his intention sincere to god in that. and likewise the angels' prayer for him, for the angels spread their wings for the seeker of knowledge in approval of what he does; and everything asks forgiveness for the scholar, even the fish in the sea. likewise in this is that a person recalls by it that he has set apart a portion of his time for the best deed that brings him near to god, glorified and exalted, and draws him close to him; so he returns with an increase of faith and a polishing of the heart and an abstemiousness towards this world and a deliverance from it, having come to know the worth of this world he is in and having come to know that it is worth nothing with god, and that the best thing in it, as the prophet, may god bless him and grant him peace, said, is knowledge — where he said: "this world is accursed, and accursed is what is in it, except the remembrance of god and what is joined to it, and a scholar or a learner." so he comes to know that the accursed thing in which there is no good is this world over which people compete, and that what god has ennobled and favoured is the revelation he sent down and the knowledge that came from him; so he sets apart a portion of his time for that. one of the sages said:

*family and ignorance dwell in one town; so either endure being parted from the family, or endure the second.*

you know the history of this community in going abroad, and how travel in the seeking of knowledge used to be, from the time of the companions of the messenger of god, may god bless him and grant him peace, to this age of ours. they used to come to him, as in the hadith of malik ibn al-huwayrith and the young men who were with him. and afterwards they used to come to one another, as in the hadith of ʿabd allah ibn unays, who travelled a month for the sake of a single hadith; and anas ibn malik, who travelled a month for the sake of a single hadith; and jabir ibn ʿabd allah, who travelled a month for the sake of a single hadith; and others of the companions who travelled for the sake of a single hadith. likewise among those after them, the successors: travel in the seeking of knowledge became famous among them and they did much of it, and likewise their followers after them; and the ages that are commended are all full of that.

so here is ahmad ibn hanbal, god's mercy upon him, saying: there did not remain a metropolis in the world in which hadith was famous but that i entered it — every metropolis of the world in which it was known that there was hadith, people occupied with hadith, he entered it. and here is al-bukhari going from nishapur heading for yemen to transmit from ʿabd al-razzaq ibn hammam al-sanʿani, even though all the hadith of ʿabd al-razzaq had reached al-bukhari with a lower chain. so he went seeking him, and when he reached mecca he was told: ʿabd al-razzaq has died. so he turned back to basra, and when he reached it he was told: ʿabd al-razzaq is alive in yemen. so he returned until he reached mecca, and there came to him one who announced ʿabd al-razzaq's death. likewise ahmad ibn hanbal and yahya ibn maʿin travelled from baghdad to sanʿaʾ on their own feet, walking, riding nothing, in the seeking of knowledge; and a great number of the people of learning did likewise. here is sahnun going out from qayrawan to medina on his feet to seek knowledge, and sitting in egypt three years in which he transmitted from ibn al-qasim what he had transmitted from malik over twenty years. when he came to ibn al-qasim he said to him: i am poor and own nothing, and the people of my country need me, and my time is short, and god has made the hajj obligatory upon me and i intend to make the pilgrimage to this house. so i want you to give me a portion of your time in which i am alone, apart from the other students; for i want to take what you took over twenty years in less than that. so he set aside a time for him, and he completed the transmission from him in three years.

likewise a number of those after them exerted remarkable effort in gathering hadith, and among the famous of them are, for example, abu zurʿah al-razi, and after him the imam al-daraqutni, and after him al-hafiz abu nuʿaym. these are among those who exerted effort for the sake of gathering hadith and attained of it what no one attained in the famous ages. and after them these two became famous: al-khatib al-baghdadi and abu ʿumar ibn ʿabd al-barr — the first the ḥāfiẓ of the east and the second the ḥāfiẓ of the west — and they died in one year. by long travel they gathered a great deal of learning. here is ibn ʿabd al-barr spending thirty years composing al-tamhīd alone, saying of it:

*the companion of my heart these thirty years, the dispeller of my care and the reliever of my distress.*

*i gathered for them in it the words of their prophet* …

and yet we find many people today being troubled and wearied over the small amounts of time one of them spends in seeking knowledge — such as a single session a week or the like — and they think the time long. and years have passed over him: did you spend these years in seeking knowledge? you did not. it was a single session a week, interrupted; whereas the lifetimes of those predecessors were like this — a single book over thirty years.

and when al-awzaʿi and his colleagues came to malik ibn anas having memorised the muwaṭṭaʾ, wanting to hear it from him, they heard it over forty days; and he said: how little understanding of it you will have — a book i composed in forty years and you take it in forty days. he is addressing the imam al-awzaʿi, who died before malik; so he was counted of the class preceding him because he died before him, but he transmitted the muwaṭṭaʾ from him.

as for the second seclusion, the seclusion of feeling, it is that a person should try, while in his dwelling and in his house, to cut out a portion of time for knowledge and to make it among his priorities, and should try to set aside for it the noblest and best of his hours — as he does that in worship and in the litany of self-examination. these are three matters which are the nourishment of the spirit and of which no one in his life can do without. first, the hour of solitude in which he worships god, glorified and exalted, and none is aware of him but the knower

of the unseen. in it he tries to worship god while people sleep, with whatever is easy, even if it be a few minutes; he recalls that in these minutes he is sharing with gabriel and michael and israfil and the bearers of the throne in the worship of god, and that by this he is alone with his lord and none but he is aware of him. by this a person crosses remarkable stages of faith, when he feels the silence around him surrounding him on every side and knows that god is aware of the innermost of his heart, and that he is worshipping him now and worshipping him with what his righteous servants worship him with, and setting himself apart for him and making himself sincere to him — this is a lofty station.

the second hour is the hour of self-examination, in which a person calls himself to account for the time that has passed, so that he calls himself to account every twenty-four hours, making them a whole lifetime. the capital is what god has given him of blessings — of faith and knowledge and strength, the strength of the limbs and the strength of the mind, and well-being in family and in security, and other things — and what he planned to do in twenty-four hours. so he calls himself to account for that and looks at what he fell short in towards god, and what he committed, and where he used god's blessing to disobey him, and hastens to repent of it and feels shame before god for having used his blessing in disobeying him. and whatever he performed of acts of obedience, let him know that it is of god's grace and mercy and granting of success and his favour and his honouring him by it and singling him out for it among others; so let him praise god for it and thank him and recall his blessing and let nothing make him forget or neglect to mention it, for god's blessing must be mentioned. many people forget the blessing of being granted success in worship; for god most high said, of the state of one he is pleased with: "praise be to god who guided us to this; we would not have been guided had god not guided us" (sūrat al-aʿrāf 7:43). so let a person recall this blessing and give thanks for it, and call himself to account for his time and for the daily plan he prepared, and look at what he fell short in and look at the cause of that.

many of the predecessors, from the intensity of their watchfulness over themselves, used to know the direction from which the error entered upon them. one of them says: a single morsel makes my heart rust, and i remain a long time treating it. a single morsel whose lawfulness is not ascertained makes the heart rust and become soiled, and he finds delusions and suspicions and doubts and many distractions in his prayer and elsewhere, and he spends a time treating them. but their inner thoughts were clear and their souls sound, and so they knew how to diagnose the diseases. as for us, diseases and symptoms have multiplied upon us, until the gazelles became so many for khirash that khirash no longer knows what he is hunting. we no longer know where we came from, nor where the flaw entered into our upbringing and our lives.

the third hour is the one we want, which is the hour of knowledge. a person ought to choose for it the time in which he finds clarity of mind and ease of heart and ease of body, and no drowsiness and no distraction. the best of that is what is at the end of the night or at the beginning of the day in the morning, for it is the blessed time in which this community has been blessed: "o god, bless my community in its early mornings." a person should try to use a quarter of an hour daily or the like in what increases him in knowledge; and if he can make himself a programme, through his own experience and through consulting his brothers and their experience, or a group of them can cooperate on that, then this is better. and whatever he is able to take of his time for seeking knowledge beyond this hour is better and more excellent for him.

the second of the conditions of seeking knowledge is humility. for knowledge is a precious commodity, and whoever has attained a precious commodity and knows people's need of it and recalls the price he spent in obtaining it — recalls the sleeplessness he used to endure and the weariness he used to bear in order to obtain it, and the hardships and dangers he took upon himself in order to reach it — cannot hand it over except to one who is humble before him. so the seeker of knowledge needs the utmost humility in order to attain his aim. the root of that is the story of moses with al-khidr, for he {said: may i follow you, that you may teach me of what you have been taught of right guidance?} (sūrat al-kahf 18:66). he said "may i follow you" and did not say "i shall follow you"; "that you may teach me" — so he made himself a student to be taught; "of what you have been taught" — that is, some of what you have been taught; he did not want to take all that he had. this is the utmost humility, and a person always needs this humility. whoever humbles himself for god, god raises him; and the prophet, may god bless him and grant him peace, commanded that, and said: "god has revealed to me that you should be humble, so that no one may transgress against another." humility is evidence of nobility of soul, unlike arrogance, which is evidence of nearness to iblis; for the root of arrogance is from him — he is the one who said: i am better than he; you created me from fire and created him from clay. and the more a person is humble, the further he is from the road of iblis.

the third of these conditions is scrupulousness (waraʿ). a person needs to go to great lengths in it in order to attain knowledge, because knowledge is a light that shies away: it is a light that shies away from darkness, and the worst darkness is the darkness of disobedience. therefore it cannot settle in the hearts of the dissolute. whoever is dissolute and does not care cannot see the light of knowledge; some of the learning may run upon his tongue, but it does not pass beyond his collarbone — as the prophet, may god bless him and grant him peace, reported of the khawarij, that they recite the qur'an and it does not pass beyond their throats. so a person needs an increase in scrupulousness in order to attain this knowledge. scrupulousness is required in every case, because of the words of the prophet, may god bless him and grant him peace, in the hadith of al-nuʿman ibn bashir, may god be pleased with them both: "the lawful is clear and the forbidden is clear, and between them are doubtful matters which many people do not know. so whoever guards against the doubtful has protected his religion and his honour; and whoever falls into the doubtful falls into the forbidden, like a shepherd who grazes around a protected pasture and is on the verge of grazing within it. truly, every king has a protected pasture; truly, god's protected pasture is what he has forbidden. truly, in the body there is a morsel of flesh: if it is sound, the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. truly, it is the heart."

his words "truly, in the body there is a morsel of flesh: if it is sound, the whole body is sound" are a notice that the soundness and corruption of the heart are according to the measure of scrupulousness in it. when scrupulousness increases, the soundness of the heart increases; and when it decreases, the soundness of the heart decreases and its corruption increases. it is related from al-shafiʿi, may god have mercy on him, that he said:

*i complained to wakiʿ of the poorness of my memory, and he directed me to leaving off acts of disobedience,*

*and told me that knowledge is a light, and the light of god is not granted to one who disobeys.*

the root of this is that whoever's scrupulousness is deficient follows his desire, and whoever follows his desire is led by that to the opposite of knowledge — because gathering knowledge is hard and entails opposing desire, since it requires of a person sleeplessness and weariness and toil and much hardship and withdrawal from appetites, and so it is contrary to desire. and whatever is contrary to desire, only one who has scrupulousness endures it; for whoever's scrupulousness is deficient must be among the followers of appetites.

the prophet, may god bless him and grant him peace, in his training, used to urge scrupulousness in food and drink and other things. in the two ṣaḥīḥs, when he saw al-hasan ibn ʿali, who was a child, take a date from the dates of charity and put it in his mouth, he took hold of him and began saying "kakh, kakh" until he threw it away, and said: we are a household to whom charity is not lawful — a single date, which he extracted from his mouth. and in the hadith of anas in ṣaḥīḥ al-bukhārī, the prophet, may god bless him and grant him peace, said: "i pass by the date and want to eat it, and then fear that it may be from the dates of charity, and so i leave it." a single date — the master of humankind, may god bless him and grant him peace, guards scrupulously against it. likewise in the two of them, from abu bakr, may god be pleased with him, that a slave of his brought him food when he was hungry and he ate of it, and the slave said to him: do you know where i got this from? he said: no. he said: i used to practise soothsaying for a people in the age of ignorance, and they saw me and made me a gift of this food. so abu bakr put his finger in, and did not stop vomiting until he had vomited everything in his stomach, out of scrupulousness about that.

scrupulousness likewise includes restraining the limbs as far as a person is able. the attempt to discipline the limbs so that they refrain from what god has forbidden them enters into scrupulousness: {say to the believing men that they lower their gaze and guard their private parts; that is purer for them. indeed god is aware of what they do} (sūrat al-nūr 24:30).

the fourth condition is hunger. for when a person is sated, that calls him to incline to this world and to increase of it. the sages used to say of old: fullness of belly takes away sharpness of mind. so the full belly takes away sharpness, and the natural talent and the intelligence are diminished. al-shafiʿi said: i have never seen an intelligent fat man except muhammad ibn al-hasan al-shaybani. the root of this from the qur'an is the words of god most high in the story of moses, peace be upon him: {he said to his young companion: bring us our morning meal; we have met from this journey of ours weariness} (sūrat al-kahf 18:62) — so he did not attain this knowledge until he met weariness and hunger from his journey.

you know that the most retentive of the companions of the prophet, may god bless him and grant him peace, of his hadith is abu hurayrah, may god be pleased with him; and that was because he was among the severest of them in poverty and need. he used to fall unconscious from hunger, so that a man would pass by him on the road to the mosque and tread on his neck, supposing him mad — and he would only be falling unconscious from hunger. nothing distracted him from memorising the hadith of the messenger of god, may god bless him and grant him peace, and so he was the most retentive of the community of it; god prepared him for that.

it is related of al-shafiʿi, may god have mercy on him, that when his mother brought him to mecca he would go to the circles of the sacred mosque and write from the hadith scholars in the mosque, such as sufyan ibn ʿuyaynah and others; and he would gather their hadith and what he wrote from them until his house was filled with the scraps he had written on. so he shut his door upon himself and did not go out until he had memorised everything in the house; and he came out in the severest degree of hunger, but he came out having memorised everything in the house, and after that had no need to carry it.

hunger is in fact an aid to memorisation: the poor are more retentive than others and the rich are the least retentive of people. memorisation is an important and indispensable means of knowledge, and for this reason god, glorified and exalted, undertook to his messenger, may god bless him and grant him peace, to preserve the qur'an for him: {do not move your tongue with it to hasten it; indeed upon us is its gathering and its recitation. so when we have recited it, follow its recitation. then indeed upon us is its clarification} (sūrat al-qiyāmah 75:16–19). likewise the prophet, may god bless him and grant him peace, urged memorisation from him, and ʿumar ibn al-khattab likewise urged memorisation in what people transmit.

al-shafiʿi, may god have mercy on him, said: proper conduct is that you write down the best of what you have heard, and memorise the best of what you have written, and relate the best of what you have memorised. so he made it three ranks: first, that you write the best of what you have heard; second, that you memorise the best of what you have written; third, that you relate the best of what you have memorised — each rank selected from the one above it. and he said, may god have mercy on him:

*my knowledge is with me wherever i turn; it follows me. my heart is its vessel, not the hollow of a chest.*

*if i am in the house, knowledge is in it with me; or if i am in the market, knowledge is in the market.*

and abu muhammad ʿali ibn hazm al-zahiri, may god most high have mercy on him, says:

*though they burn the paper, they will not burn what the paper contained; it is rather in my breast.*

*it travels with me wherever my mounts set out, and it stays if i stay, and it will be buried in my grave.*

the scholars used to say: what the book-case holds is not knowledge; knowledge is only what the breast holds. so the broad shelves with many coloured books on them are not knowledge; knowledge is only what the breast holds. therefore a person needs the instruments of memorisation and the strengthening of that in his mind, so that this may increase him in insight and skill and in gathering the scattered parts and edges of knowledge; and that is accomplished only by hunger at the stage of memorisation.

what is meant by that is moderation in the matter. it is not meant as tormenting the self and starving it, nor as reducing food to the point that it becomes harmful to a person and a diminishing of his strength or a means to his illness. rather what is meant is that a person be moderate in that and not make this his greatest concern, and that he not spend the best of his time in obtaining his food; rather the best of the time must be what he spends in obtaining knowledge.

the fifth condition is realising the importance of knowledge, which is that a person should hold himself cheap for the sake of gathering knowledge. for whoever does not realise the importance of a thing cannot occupy himself with it, since whoever is ignorant of a thing is hostile to it. that is why you find that many people, when they have tasted the taste of knowledge, become absorbed in it and it delights them, until many others who have not tasted the taste of knowledge consider them men of obsession who have plunged into a matter in which they ought to have kept to the middle and not exceeded. the fact is that they have tasted this taste and the others have not tasted it; or that they have seen this flash and others have not seen it. for this reason moses, peace be upon him, held himself cheap for the sake of knowledge and rode the sea in a holed ship. one of the scholars said of old:

*the questions of sahnun said to their reader: you will not attain knowledge until you lick aloes.*

*knowledge is not attained by an idler, nor by a sluggard, nor by one easily bored, nor by one who keeps company with people.*

"the questions of sahnun" is al-mudawwanah, and people used to memorise it as they memorise al-fātiḥah. "until you lick aloes" — that is, until you lick what is intensely bitter. but for all that, patience under slight weariness brings a person afterwards to attain stations he would not have attained without this, as the sage said: *no face has become white by the gaining of a noble thing until it was first darkened by the pallor of the quest.*

so if you see one whose face has become white by any noble thing, know that that was preceded by weariness and toil.

the sixth condition is disobeying desire. for one who lets his soul follow its desire must be afflicted with wishful thinking and suspicions; while one who does not follow desire, when his soul inclines to anything, calls it to account for it and holds it under suspicion in it — this is the one who is able to gather knowledge. that is why abu ʿasim al-nabil, when he was hearing hadith from shuʿbah, and the elephants came to the land of kufa in the countryside of iraq and the students of hadith went out to look at the elephants — shuʿbah said to abu ʿasim: will you not go out to the elephants? he said: i did not come to see the elephants; i came only to write hadith. so he nicknamed him "the noble" because of that. and al-suyuti, may god have mercy on him, mentions that he had a window overlooking the nile, and that when the nile flooded people would come to it from distant lands to see its flood; and he remained sixteen years without opening the window to see the nile, because of his occupation with knowledge — sixteen years. so a person must try not to follow desire, even in permissible matters, so that he may attain knowledge in exchange for that.

the seventh condition is acting upon it. for knowledge, as ibn ʿuyaynah said, calls out for action: if it answers it, well; otherwise it departs. so whoever does not act upon what he knows, it is a proof against him; and whoever acts upon what he knows, god grants him knowledge of what he did not know. god most high says: {o you who believe, if you are mindful of god he will make for you a criterion} (sūrat al-anfāl 8:29). and the criterion is that by which a person distinguishes between truth and falsehood, and it is a knowledge bestowed directly from god.

al-bukhari and muslim brought out in the two ṣaḥīḥs, and others, from the hadith of abu juhayfah al-suwaʾi, may god be pleased with him, who said: we said to ʿali ibn abi talib, may god be pleased with him: do you have anything that you recite other than the book of god? he said: by him who split the seed and created the soul, we have nothing that we recite other than the book of god and what is in this sheet — or an understanding that god grants to a man among his servants. and he brought out the sheet from the scabbard of his sword, and in it was the blood-money, and the ransoming of the captive, and that a muslim is not killed for an unbeliever, and: medina is a sanctuary from ʿāʾir to such-and-such, and whoever commits an offence in it or shelters an offender, upon him is the curse of god and of the angels and of all people; god will not accept from him any obligatory or voluntary act. and whoever claims a father other than his own, or affiliates to other than his own patrons, upon him is the curse of god and of the angels and of all people; god will not accept from him any obligatory or voluntary act … and so on.

the point of citation in the hadith is ʿali's words "or an understanding that god grants to a man among his servants". this understanding is the knowledge bestowed directly, and it is the second side of knowledge. for knowledge divides into two kinds: knowledge by jidd (earnest effort) and knowledge by jadd (good fortune). the knowledge that is by earnest effort is what is attained by striving and expenditure; and knowledge by good fortune, that is by felicity, is that with which god makes felicitous whomever he wills of his servants, and it is a result of action. the divine lights and the outpourings which the devoted worshippers attain often fill a great gap in the field of knowledge. god most high has said: {and david and solomon, when they gave judgement concerning the tillage, when the sheep of the people strayed into it at night; and we were witnesses to their judgement. and we gave solomon understanding of it; and to each we gave judgement and knowledge} (sūrat al-anbiyāʾ 21:78–79). this granting of understanding is a divine outpouring and a divine light which god cast into the heart of solomon, so that by it he understood god's ruling.

ʿumar ibn al-khattab, may god most high be pleased with him, used to say: o god, i seek refuge with you from a difficult case for which there is no abu hasan — meaning ʿali, may god be pleased with him; for he used to solve the difficult cases. whoever reads his life, may god be pleased with him, knows that much of the knowledge he had was not among the acquired sciences that human beings reach by striving and seeking; rather it must be a knowledge bestowed directly and divinely, arising from acting upon what he learned and from an increase of faith and god-consciousness and scrupulousness. for he, may god be pleased with him, was one day on the pulpit, and a man stood up and said: a man has died leaving a wife, two parents and two daughters. and ʿali — and he was in the middle of a sermon rhyming in ʿayn — said: her eighth has become a ninth. the beginning of his sermon was: praise be to god, who recompenses every soul for what it strives for, and to him is the return and the coming back. so the questioner asked

about this, and he said: her eighth has become a ninth. from that time it has been known as "the pulpit inheritance case" (al-farīḍah al-minbariyyah), and in it he set out the increase of twenty-four to twenty-seven. for twenty-four is the third of the bases that admit of increase, and its increase is one: it increases only to twenty-seven and nothing else increases. this was not known before this occasion — it was not known in islam before that occasion — and he produced it with this spontaneity and this speed and said: her eighth has become a ninth.

these seven conditions one of the scholars versified in a single line, saying:

*for it: go abroad, and be humble, and be scrupulous, and be hungry, and be weak, and disobey your desire, and follow.*

knowledge is of many kinds, and among the greatest of them is the knowledge of practised skill; for knowledge divides into two kinds, the knowledge of receiving and the knowledge of practised skill. the knowledge of receiving means what a person receives from another; and of this kind, some is what he hears and so receives by way of the ear, and some is what he receives by way of writing, and some is what he receives by way of looking and observing alone — all of that is of the knowledge of receiving. as for the knowledge of practised skill, which is the knowledge of training, it is what a person acquires from experience and by which he is able to express what is in his breast and convey his knowledge to another. for how many a person's breast contains much learning but he is unable to express it; and how many a person is a parrot who has come to know learning by rote and repeats it as he took it — "this is our merchandise returned to us". these two kinds are deficient, and the third kind is better, namely the one who develops and adds and improves.

a man saw three doves: one of them swallowed a jewel and brought it out as it was; another swallowed it and brought it out larger than it had been; and another swallowed it and brought it out smaller than it had been. so he asked muhammad ibn sirin, may god have mercy on him, about the interpretation of his dream, and he said: you sit in my session, and in the session of qatadah, and in the session of al-hasan — these are the leading successors in basra at that time. he said: yes. so he said: the dove that swallowed the jewel and brought it out larger than it had been is al-hasan al-basri, because he memorises the hadith and then adds to it by his intelligence and his acumen and his understanding and his learning. the one that brought it out as it was is qatadah, for he memorises the hadith and relates it as it is without addition or omission. and the one that brought it out smaller than it had been is i — meaning himself, muhammad ibn sirin — for i have memorised the hadith but i scruple to bring all of it, for fear of adding to it what is not of it.

in general, the one who develops his information and is able to deliver it as is fitting is without doubt better and greater in reward, because there is written for him the rewards of everyone who acts upon what he taught and the rewards of those to whom anything of his learning reached, until the day of resurrection, without that diminishing anything of their rewards. this is the aspect in which the predecessors were given precedence over the later generations: that their rewards are not cut off but increase according to the centuries. my teacher, may god have mercy on him, said:

*and every reward attained by the martyrs, or by others such as the scholars and the ascetics,*

*there is attained for the prophet the like of it, over and above the rewards of what the prophet himself did,*

*with an additional number that is not bounded and whose count none can reckon but the one;*

*for every guided person and every scholar, until the day of recompense, his teacher has attained*

*from the reward the like of the reward of the doer — and likewise from the deficient and the perfect;*

*and his teacher's teacher has twice as much, and fourfold for the third who follows him;*

*and so the doubling of every rank, up to the messenger of god, of lofty rank.*

*from this is known the precedence of the predecessors and their priority in merit over the later generations.*

therefore the person who wants to learn must add to that another intention, namely that he should teach what he has learned, because of the words of the prophet, may god bless him and grant him peace: "the best of you is he who learns the qur'an and teaches it." and that is accomplished only by several matters and several means.

the most important of them is the intention of that at the beginning. for one who studies only to learn and understand will make light of many matters and will not take on training and practised skill, because he wants only understanding and passes over that. but one who wants to learn in order to teach will attend to the manners and the conditions and the ways of delivering information and the ways of developing it and of combining it with other information, and to the difficulties that arise with it and the answers to those difficulties; and will apply that to the reality of people, so as to bring solutions for what they are thinking about and for the problems that arise for them; and will look inward into the souls of those present and listening, so as to know which of them has grasped the lesson and which has not. by this he is able to live with the lesson and in its shade. for the intention of teaching, accompanying the intention of learning, is an important matter in this field.

second, it is necessary after this that a person know that what he will teach must be less than what he has learned: he delivers to his students only a part of what he has, because if he drains everything he has he becomes an empty box. because of that he will select from what he has the easiest and the smoothest and the most firmly established, and that is what he presents, and he keeps for himself a reserve which he can develop and increase. that is why the people of learning say: knowledge is a sea, and its vessels are like the vessels of water — one scoops with them, and there cannot be a vessel that scoops the whole sea. therefore a person needs to learn more than he teaches. whoever wants to explain a particular book must be acquainted with a broader book in the discipline he is in; if you have not read a book broader than this, you will not be able to teach this book.

hence you hear of many simpletons who venture upon the great encyclopaedias and the mighty books, wanting to explain them, when those are the last thing composed in the discipline — as though they had studied what is broader than them, whereas the reality is otherwise. you find one of them venturing, for example, upon explaining the book of sibawayh, as though he had studied something broader than it in grammar; or venturing upon teaching al-muwāfaqāt of al-shatibi, as though he had studied many of the books of legal theory until he reached this rare quintessence. none will reach this level but the rarest of people, who have combined the rational and the transmitted sciences and have taken on training and gathered many disciplines and sciences. therefore, god have mercy on one who knows his measure and sits below it. the arabs say: "bow your head, kara; the ostriches are in the villages." so a person should not try to be a raisin before he is a sour grape: let him first try to bring the little before the much.

that is why ibn ʿabbas, may god be pleased with them both, said in explaining the words of god most high "be rabbānīs" (sūrat āl ʿimrān 3:79): he said, be scholars, wise men; and in another transmission: the rabbānīs are those who train people with the small matters of learning before the great ones — he tries to bring the small before the great.

for this reason the methods of the people of learning in all the sciences are that they made graded books. notice that a single author composes several books of differing sizes and differing content, intending by that the differing levels of students. here is ibn qudamah in hanbali fiqh — and he is the father of this school, its greatest compiler — who composed, for example, al-ʿumdah for the young, and above it al-muqniʿ, and above that al-kāfī, and above that al-mughnī, each book composed for one level of the students of knowledge. likewise ibn hisham al-ansari composed in grammar qaṭr al-nadā for beginners, and above it shudhūr al-dhahab, then above that iʿrāb al-jumal wa-mā yalḥaqu bihā, and above that awḍaḥ al-masālik, and above that mughnī al-labīb ʿan kutub al-aʿārīb — all this by gradation, so that the student of knowledge may proceed by degrees and not take knowledge at random. many people do not grasp this division and so fall upon the largest books they find, and hold that the small books are of no benefit and are a waste of time, and pass them by.
