and there is no doubt that the other great collections of the sunnah are not free of these reports. ṣaḥīḥ al-bukhārī has a great number of them in it; ṣaḥīḥ muslim likewise has a number, less than that; the books of the sunan have many of them; and the muwaṭṭaʾ has many of them. so the study of these reports is easy, exactly like the study of the reports traced to the prophet. but some contemporary researchers — indeed many of them — give attention to tracing the hadiths and passing judgement on them, while as for the transmitted reports, they generally pass no judgement on them; and this is a methodological error that certain universities existing today have adopted. but i see no ground for it: from the point of view of correctness, there is no difference between it and the hadiths. many of these reports, if a person does not find them in the books we have mentioned, he can go back to the biographical works, and to the books that take care to bring forward the narrations of the transmitters, such as al-kāmil of ibn adi — for he takes care to bring forward the narrations of every transmitter. likewise even in al-iṣābah, for example, of al-hafiz ibn hajar, he sometimes takes care to give the narration from each one; and likewise even al-dhahabi before him takes care with some of the reports narrated from some of those whose lives he records.

likewise ibn sa'd in his book al-ṭabaqāt brings forward many reports from many of the companions and successors whose lives he records. and some books of qur'anic exegesis too give the chains of transmission for the reports — such as the book of al-tabari, and the book of al-nasa'i, and the book of abd al-rahman ibn abi hatim al-razi: they bring forward the reports with their chains back to those who said them, and then there is no problem.

but if a person finds no chain for the report at all, let him search for it in the other books that are rarely to be found, such as al-ʿilal of al-daraqutni, and al-ʿilal of ibn abi hatim al-razi, and al-marāsīl of ibn abi hatim, and al-marāsīl of abu dawud. for by these "mursal" reports they often mean reports that are not mursal in the technical sense of hadith; rather they mean by them the transmitted reports.

the question here is about the other kharijite sects besides the ibadis — whether anything of their books has survived. the answer is that the last of the kharijite sects besides the ibadis is the sufriyyah, and it was effaced in the fifth century of the hijrah and no trace of it remained. as for before that, the other kharijite sects — such as the azariqah, and such as the tarifiyyah, the followers of al-walid ibn tarif, and such as a number of other sects — were effaced and nothing of them remained. as for the effect of creed upon compositions and methods, it is very clear and great. for this reason al-shafi'i (may god have mercy on him) said in al-umm: "i do not reject the testimony of a witness from among the people of the qiblah, nor his narration" — he means in testimonies, and by "narration" in reports of fact, not in hadith: if he says he has seen the new moon, or the like — "except the khattabiyyah, for they hold it lawful to lie in testimony for anyone who agrees with them in their sect." the khattabiyyah alone have their testimony rejected absolutely. and there is no doubt that in the ja'fariyyah, the imami school, much lying and fabrication is notorious; but that fabrication comes from the great heads, while as for those below them, they hold those books in great sanctity and cannot dare to change anything in them. as for the kharijites, they hold that lying is unbelief, and so they take care over exactness in transmission; and yet even so their books too are not free of some weak and fabricated material, and they often rely on extremely flimsy things — as do the people of the sunnah also, for among the people of the sunnah there is to be found the adducing of extremely flimsy hadiths as evidence.

as for the question here about the school of the ibadis and the zaydis, that these two are said to be the closest of the schools of the innovators to the people of the sunnah —

as for the question about imam al-shawkani, whether he is an absolute practitioner of independent legal reasoning or a dependent one:

the answer is that the lateness of his time prevented him from the rank of absolute independent legal reasoning, because there remained nothing new that he could say in the field of legal theory: all that he does is to piece together the statements of those who preceded him. the parallel to this is what we mentioned earlier about shaykh al-islam ibn taymiyyah — with the vast distance between the two of them in time, in scholarly standing and in other respects. for if we say that shaykh al-islam ibn taymiyyah does not reach the rank of absolute independent legal reasoning, then what of al-shawkani? the point is that the possibilities in legal theory which minds can entertain have come to an end; so the mere piecing together of them cannot make the one who does it an absolute practitioner of independent reasoning, because something of the words of those before him must inevitably come out preponderant with him — sometimes by looking to its evidence, sometimes by the number of those who hold it, and sometimes he goes back on his preference to prefer the other side of the scale, and so on. for this reason al-shawkani (may god have mercy on him) — most of his books are summaries of the books of those who went before. his book in legal theory, irshād al-fuḥūl, as we shall mention, god willing, among the books of legal theory, is a summary of the book al-baḥr al-muḥīṭ of al-zarkashi; and his book in qur'anic exegesis is a summary of the book of al-qurtubi and the book of al-suyuti, which he combined in it — al-durr al-manthūr is the exegesis of al-qurtubi — and so on in his other books: he always attempts summarising and combining. for this reason, in legal theory he sometimes holds a position preponderant and then forgets that he held it preponderant, and in the following question holds preponderant something built upon the other position, the one he had held to be outweighed in the previous question. this happened to him in a number of places in irshād al-fuḥūl.

the question here is about the claim that absolute independent legal reasoning was sealed with the imams of the four schools — whether it is correct or not correct.

the answer is that it is not correct, because after them came dawud al-zahiri, and after them came muhammad ibn jarir al-tabari, and there is no doubt that the two of them brought new positions. but the problem here is that some of those who innovated positions in legal theory were followers of the schools, who did not reach in jurisprudence the rank of absolute independent reasoning, nor in hadith, nor in exegesis, but who innovated in legal theory. these are the likes of abu bakr al-baqillani in the maliki school — for there is no doubt that he was an innovator in legal theory and brought new things that the malikis did not have before; and like him al-afri, and ibn al-qassar, and ibn khuwayz mindad, who brought new things not found among the malikis before. and likewise al-qarafi among the later scholars, and al-shatibi after him: these brought new things not found among the early malikis. but their qualification in the other sciences did not enable them to reach absolute independent reasoning, and so they remained within the school. and likewise in the other schools: for example al-qadi husayn, and abu al-ma'ali al-juwayni, and al-ghazali, and fakhr al-din al-razi, and al-amidi in the shafi'i school — there is no doubt that they brought many new things in legal theory, but their qualifications in the other matters did not raise them to going outside the shafi'i school; and so on. so the point here is a matter of specialisations. completeness is difficult; and those in whom completeness was achieved, to the rank that brings its possessors to absolute independent reasoning, were in later ages in which the possibilities did not remain open.

for this reason there is no doubt that the age of ibn taymiyyah was at that time a very great scholarly renaissance, and especially in syria and egypt; and there appeared in it very great giants in various sciences, and he studied under a number of them and gathered up much of what they had. at that time, for example, in hadith there was al-hafiz al-mizzi — there is no doubt that he gathered and stored up — and his students likewise. likewise al-haythami: there is no doubt that he is among the most comprehensive of people in hadith and the most far-reaching of them in acquaintance with it. and likewise in the appraisal of narrators, al-hafiz al-dhahabi is the wonder of the world in the narrators; he has no equal in islam in the science of narrators. and after these came their students — for example al-hafiz zayn al-din al-iraqi in hadith, and he himself said: "i met a number of the great memorisers, and i have left behind me only two." he says at the end of his life: "there remain in the world only two great memorisers: my son abu zur'ah" — his son is al-wali, wali al-din — "and ahmad ibn ali ibn hajar al-asqalani, al-hafiz." he said: "there remain in the world none but these two great memorisers." then after ibn hajar there came a number of great memorisers whose standing was high, such as al-dimi, and such as al-sakhawi, and such as ibn fahd al-makki, and such as al-muhibb al-tabari, and such as al-suyuti. these eminent men memorised everything. al-suyuti's memory in the base texts was extremely remarkable; and al-dimi was likewise remarkable in hadith; and al-sakhawi in the narrators and the hidden defects of hadith.

question: what is the reason for the spread of the hanafi school, despite its relying on considered opinion? is it merely that the governments were founded upon it and supported it, or does it have an intrinsic strength in the school itself that entails this?

the answer: that its relying on considered opinion is, as we said earlier, a mere convention of terminology. otherwise, it is not possible that this great school, which agrees with many of the hadiths and whose evidences now run to thousands of hadiths, should be built upon considered opinion alone. that is why one of the hanafi debaters, namely imam al-ayni, when one of the scholars of egypt debated with him and said to him: "abu hanifah narrated only thirteen hadiths" — he said: "this is a distinction belonging to abu hanifah the like of which is no distinction at all. if he produced all these questions of jurisprudence in agreement with the hadith of the prophet (may god bless him and grant him peace) while not knowing it, that means that he is in agreement with the hadith. umar ibn al-khattab agreed with the revelation in a few questions, and it was a great distinction for him — so what of abu hanifah, who agreed with it in thousands of questions? thousands of questions among the hanafis are in agreement with the sound hadiths. if he did not know the hadiths, and it was merely his intellect that led him to agree with the revelation, this is an extremely great distinction; and if he did know them, then how can you say this?"

so the matter is not to be taken without qualification. the hanafis — their school is like the other schools, and their evidences are not other than like the evidences of the others. if you go back to the hadiths upon which islam turns — for example eleven thousand hadiths on the rulings — these are distributed among the schools, and no school's share of them is greater than another school's share. for this reason the adherents of every school took care to gather its evidences; and we have mentioned that among the best books on the tracing of evidences is naṣb al-rāyah of the hanafis, by al-zayla'i: it is among the best books on tracing, the tracing of the evidences. and this although the malikis, who were renowned for memorising hadith and for expertise in it, laboured and laboured exceedingly in gathering their evidences, and their books do not reach al-zayla'i's level. for example, the books of al-hafiz abd al-haqq al-ishbili — al-aḥkām al-kubrā, al-aḥkām al-wusṭā and al-aḥkām al-ṣughrā — despite his own labour, and he was a colossal memoriser who used to memorise a hundred thousand hadiths with their chains and their texts and dictate them to people by dictation; and yet his books now have not the renown in islam that al-zayla'i's book has, even though people flew with his books east and west, and all the schools relied upon them. and abu al-hasan ibn al-qattan al-fasi composed the book bayān al-wahm wa-l-īhām, in which he tracked the errors of abd al-haqq al-ishbili in al-aḥkām al-wusṭā; and this book too is among the prominent and powerful books on the hidden defects of hadith, relied upon by al-hafiz ibn hajar, for example, and by those below him. on this basis the matter is always relative.

as for this matter of which it is said that they reject hadith by considered opinion: this matter too is not to be taken without qualification, it is not as it is made out. a person must look carefully and know what is meant in each case. the hanafis have rules upon which there are many mass-transmitted evidences, and these rules they made into governing principles and tried to refer the whole of the sharia back to them. so these rules [are applied] by three measures; and when they find an anomalous branch that is an exception, they call it juristic preference (istiḥsān), an exception from the rules. and so, when they find a great number of mass-transmitted reports on one side and find a hadith that contradicts it, upon which practice is not established, they abandon acting upon the hadith — and this is not peculiar to them; rather this is found among the malikis, and among the hanbalis, and among the shafi'is, many parallels to it.

as for what was mentioned about the hadith of the two large jars (qullatayn): as for the hadith itself, i am convinced that it is not authentically established from the prophet (may god bless him and grant him peace), for several reasons. the hadith turns on muhammad ibn ishaq and al-walid ibn abi kathir. malik's words about muhammad ibn ishaq are well known, and the words of others also. and al-walid ibn abi kathir was an ibadi kharijite. and both of them were differed over in it: sometimes the two of them narrate it from muhammad ibn abbad ibn ja'far ibn al-zubayr, and sometimes from muhammad ibn ja'far ibn al-zubayr. then each one of these two was differed over in it: sometimes they narrate it from abd allah ibn abd allah ibn umar, in the enlarged form of the name, and sometimes from ubayd allah ibn abd allah ibn umar, in the diminutive form.

then, after that, it is unstable in its text; for in it there is: "when the water reaches two jars, or three", in the sunan of al-tirmidhi; and in it there is: "when the water reaches a hundred jars", and this is in the sunan of al-daraqutni. and also, the jars are not of a determined measure — especially as nothing has come regarding their measure except what al-bayhaqi mentioned, that they are of the jars of hajar; and this in fact turns upon al-mughirah ibn saqlab, and al-mughirah ibn saqlab is weak in the view of all the people of hadith. so there is no account to be taken of this measure.

then, after that, in the wording of the hadith too there is a difficulty. the hadith is from ibn umar, that the prophet (may god bless him and grant him peace) was asked about water that lies in open desert country and about the beasts of prey and the animals that come to it, and he said: "when the water reaches two jars, it does not carry filth." what is the meaning of "does not carry"? "does not carry filth" — what is the meaning of this word? so the difficulty is present in any case. for this reason the hanafis' abandoning it is not merely a case of abandoning a hadith by considered opinion; rather, from the point of view of the hadith discipline: first, its soundness — it is not sound; second, from the point of view of measure, there is nothing that fixes the measure of the two jars. and even if we were to say that al-mughirah ibn saqlab's narration, if a corroborating narration or a supporting witness were found for it and we declared it sound — which is not possible — the jars of hajar are of varying sizes. that is why the prophet (may god bless him and grant him peace) likened to them the fruits of the lote-tree of the utmost boundary, saying: "and its leaves are like the ears of elephants, and its fruits are like the jars of hajar." and the fruit of the lote-tree is always of varying size; and so likewise the jars of hajar.

the question here: how do we arrive at the preponderant position in the hanbali school when the narrations are multiple?

the answer is that this is what a number of the leading authorities occupied themselves with, and among the most important of that is al-mardawi's book al-inṣāf; for he attempts to gather the narrations and then to make clear to you which of them is the school's position. and among the later scholars there are likewise supplements to it and follow-ups to it; but al-mardawi's book is among the most important books in this field.

a question about certain modern tendencies in studies that take care to gather the jurisprudence of certain of the early authorities on particular questions and give them this title, "the jurisprudence of so-and-so", of the companions or of the successors or of those who followed them.

a question as to whether this work may make it easier for the researcher to become acquainted with the views of the companions and the successors — whether that is correct.

the answer: yes, if that is in books of transmitted reports; if that is in gathering books of transmitted reports which gather the statements of a number of people, so as to cover a large area of jurisprudence. but if it is merely for the statements of one particular person, and we want to make a complete school for him — for example, we arrange chapters for him like the chapters of jurisprudence: the chapter on ritual purity and what is narrated from sa'id in it, and the chapter on prayer, and the chapter on zakat, and so on — then this is not correct. for they do not have exercises of independent reasoning that cover these areas; indeed, with many of them, what is narrated from them in many of the great books of jurisprudence may be one question or two questions or thereabouts. so this is an injustice to them and a wrong done to them. for this reason those who occupy themselves with this kind of study will take from every tom and dick, and will generate questions, and will go hunting for the fallen and the gored and what the wild beast has eaten, in order to patch up the chapters of jurisprudence.

the second question, about the fact that some ill-intentioned people, when they look into jurisprudence and find the many disagreements and the refutations
r:
ذكر الشيخ عبد الفتاح أبو غدة في كتابه صفحات من صبر العلماء، قصص عجيبة في حرص بعض العلماء على بعض الكتب النادرة وعنايتهم بها، وذكر قصة جرت له هو، كان يبحث عن كتاب فبحث عنه في كل مكتبات مصر ومكتبات الشام ومكتبات الهند وما وجده، وذكر له رجل أنه بمكتبة في مكة، فطار فرحا بذلك فذهب إلى المكتبة فوجد صاحب المكتبة فقال هذا الكتاب كانت عندي منه نسخة واحدة واشتراها رجل شنقيطي معمم أتى بالأمس فاشتراه.

فحزن حزنا شديدا فما نام، حزنا لذلك، ثم ذهب إلى الكعبة وطاف وهو يدعو أن يجد هذا الرجل ولا يعرف له اسما ولا صفة إلا أنه شنقيطي معمم، فكان كلما رأى من عليه عمامة سأله حتى وجد الرجل ووجد الكتاب عنده فاستعاره منه.

وكانوا يحرصون أيضا على استعارة الكتب من الناس، وكثير من العلماء كانوا يكرهون إعارة الكتب، لتعرضها للضياع بذلك، ولهذا فإن المختار بن بونه رحمه الله لما كان يؤلف الجامع بين التسهيل والخلاصة المانع من الحشو والخصاصة، لم يكن عنده شرح الدماميني على التسهيل وهو من أهم كتب النحو، ذهب يطلبه فأتى قوما من أهل المكتبات في البلاد من قبيلة العلويين فأنشدهم أبياتا يقول فيها:..

يا ابن المشايخ والأشياخ أسلافه *** إن تبصرة الحكام مبخلة

ومن أعار سواد القلب أتلفه ...

ولهذا فإن أسد بن الفرات كما ذكرنا من قبل امتنع من إعارة مدونته لسحنون حتى يقابل عليها، فأعاره إياها ليلة واحدة فوزعها سحنون على الطلاب فكتبوها كلها في تلك الليلة.

هذا السؤال عن مصطلحات المذاهب؟

لا شك أن لكل مذهب مصطلحات تدور في المذهب كله في كتبه، ومصطلحات مختصة للمؤلفين في كتبهم، وهذا النوع الأخير يعتني به شراح كل كتاب، فمثلا في المذهب الحنبلي يعتني الناس ببعض المصطلحات التي يكثر دورانها في المذهب وبالأخص في كلام ابن قدامة وشراح كتبه، فمثلا عند الحنابلة الروايتان والوجهان والقولان والرواية المخرجة والشيخ مثلا ونحو ذلك من المصطلحات المعروفة لديهم، وكذلك عند الشافعية أصحاب الوجوه والقولان والجديد والقديم، وكذلك عند الحنفية وجه الرواية والزيادات والنوادر وكذلك عند المالكية كثير من المصطلحات جدا من هذا النوع، ومصطلحات المالكية ما كان منها متعلقا بالكتب ألف فيه بعض الكتب المختصة مثل رفع نقاب الحاجب عن مصطلحات ابن الحاجب، مصطلحات فقط في مختصر ابن الحاجب جامع الأمهات ألف فيه ابن فرحون كتابه رفع نقاب الحاجب عن مصطلحات ابن الحاجب.

وكذلك فإن خليلا رحمه الله في مقدمة المختصر ذكر مصطلحاته في الكتاب غالبا، وأهمل بعضها، فإنه يقول فيه: يقول العبد الفقير المضطر لرحمة ربه المنكسر خاطره لقلة العمل والتقوى خليل بن إسحاق بن موسى المالكي رحمه الله تعالى: الحمد لله حمدا يوافي ما تزايد من النعم والشكر له على ما أولانا من الفضل والكرم، لا أحصي ثناء عليه هو كما أثنى على نفسه، ونسأله اللطف والإعانة في جميع الأحوال وحال حلول الإنسان في رمسه، والصلاة والسلام على نبينا محمد سيد العرب والعجم المبعوث لسائر الأمم، وعلى آله وأصحابه، وبعد فقد سألني جماعة أبان الله لي ولهم معالم التحقيق، وسلك بنا وبهم أنفع طريق مختصرا على مذهب الإمام مالك بن أنس، مبينا لما به الفتوى، فأجبت سؤالهم بعد الاستخارة مشيرا فيها للمدونة وبأول لاختلاف شارحيها في فهمها، وبالاختيار للخمي لكن إن كان بصيغة الفعل فذلك لاختياره هو في نفسه وبالاسم فذلك لاختياره من الخلاف، وبالترجيح لابن يونس كذلك، وبالظهور لابن رشد كذلك وبالقول للمازري كذلك، وحيث قلت خلاف فذلك للاختلاف في التشهير وحيث ذكرت قولين أو أقوالا فذلك لعدم اطلاعي في الفرع على أرجحية منصوصة، وأعتبر من المفاهيم مفهوم الشرط فقط، وأشير بصحح أو استحسن إلى أن شيخا غير الذين قدمتهم قد صحح هذا أو استظهره، وبلو إلى خلاف مذهبي والله أسأل أن ينفع به من كتبه أو قرأه أو حصله أو سعى في شيء منه، ثم أعتذر لذوي الألباب من التقصير الواقع في هذا الكتاب، فقلما يخلص المصنف من الهفوات أو ينجو مؤلف من العبرات.

هنا ذكر مصطلحه في الكتاب في الغالب وأهمل بعض المصطلحات مثل إشارته بــإن إلى خلاف خارج المذهب، ومثل إشارته بطي الخلاف إلى أن القول غير المطوي هو الراجح عنده، وهكذا فلديه بعض المصطلحات القليلة التي أهملها وهي موجودة في شراحه، هذا هو أهم المصطلحات.

لدى بعض المؤلفين مصطلحات أخرى بمثابة الاختصار لأسماء بعض الكتب أو المؤلفين، وهذه المصطلحات مشكلة لأنها رموز بالحروف فقط، مثل ابن عبد الهادي الحنبلي في كتابه الفقهي يشير للمذاهب بالحروف، فالهاء لأبي حنيفة والميم لمالك والشين للشافعي ويشير كذلك لبعض علماء الحنابلة ببعض الحروف، وهذا النوع أخذ عن الغزالي في كتابه الوجيز، ثم تبعه عليه عدد من المؤلفين في الفقه، وأصبح كثير من الكتب تختصر بإشارات، وقد سلك ذلك أيضا بعض شراح الحديث، فمثلا الأبي في شرحه لصحيح مسلم إكمال الإكمال وهو إكمال لإكمال المعلم للقاضي عياض الذي هو إكمال لشرح المازري المعلم يشير فيه بالحروف إشارات، فالميم للمازري والعين لعياض وكذلك فإن السنوسي الذي ألف تكملة إكمال الإكمال أيضا يشير لكل شراح مسلم كل واحد يشير له بحرف، فالنون للنووي والباء للأبي وهكذا، كل شارح من الشراح يشير له بحرف من الحروف، هذا النوع من المصطلحات يصعب الإحاطة به، لكن في المذهب المالكي مثلا يشتهر إشارات بالحروف لدى المتأخرين لبعض المؤلفين مثلا عج لعلي الأجهوري، ومن لمحمد البناني، وصر لناصر الدين اللقاني، ومس لمصطفى المسناوي، وكذلك القاف للمواق والحاء للحطاب وهكذا، فكثير من الحروف هي إشارات رموز لبعض المؤلفين أو المؤلفات، واشتهرت حتى أصبح بعض الناس ينظمها في نظمه كما هي، مثل قول الناظم:

وكل ما تشرع فيه البسمله كما لبن..؛ أي للبناني.

ومثل قول محمد مولود في آداب الصلاة يقول:

وعج ومن تبعه قد اعتمد ...

عج يقصد به عليا الأجهوري، كذلك قوله: سر وصر، سر الميسر وصر ناصر الدين اللقاني، وكذلك ضح إشارة للتوضيح اختصار للتوضيح لخليل بن إسحاق شرح جامع الأمهات لابن الحاجب وهكذا، هذه المصطلحات يكثر دورانها في كتب المتأخرين، وهذه المصطلحات إذا لم يبينها المؤلفثم إن الخلافة العثمانية أخذت اليونينية من مصر وذهبت بها إلى إسطنبول لطباعة صحيح البخاري عليها، وهذا مثلا ابن دريد بقرهويدعي من حمقه وهو كتاب العين إلـا أنه مع هذا لا يستطيع الطعن في كتاب الجمهرة، وابن دريد يرد على نفطويه فيقول:

أف على النحو وأشياعه أحرقه الله بنصف اسمه وهو نفط ويه، فأبو علي القالي روى الكتاب عن مؤلفه وكان يحبه حبا شديدا فلما افتقر باع الكتاب مكرها وكتب على الصفحة الأولى منه هذه الأبيات:

أنست بها عشرين عاما وبعتها وما كان ظني أنني سأبيعها ولكن لعجز وافتقار وصبية وقد تحرج الحاجات يا أم مالك. ثم بعد ذلك عندما استغنى وجد الكتاب فاشتراه.

بالنسبة لأتباع المذهب الظاهري كانوا ذوي عدد في أماكن مختلفة، لكن يختلف انتشار المذهب بحسب قوة الشيخ أو العالم الذي يعتمدون عليه ويكون ركيزتهم في البلد، فإذا كان لهم علامة مشهور في بلد من البلدان كثر الأتباع أتباع المذهب، وإلا فهم يمكن أن يكونوا نصف أهل السنة من ناحية التصور العقلي، لأنهم الوحيدون من أهل السنة الذين لا يثبتون القياس، فلذلك يمكن إذا رجعت إلى التقسيم العقلي تجد أهل السنة مثبتة قياس ونفاة قياس، فالواقع في مجال القياس ما لأهل السنة إلا مذهبان مذهب المثبتة ومذهب النفاة، وقد كانوا ذوي عدد في أماكن مختلفة من العالم، في المشرق وفي المغرب.

بالنسبة لدقة بعض المذاهب التي أصحابها أصحاب بدعة، أو إحسانهم في التأليف في مجالاتهم لا يقتضي ذلك الفتنة بما لديهم، فالمذاهب كما ذكرنا من قبل هي مجرد طرق للتعامل مع النصوص، ولهذا ففيها الحق والباطل، فيها الصواب والخطأ فلا يمكن أن يتبع أي مجتهد حتى ولو كان أبا بكر الصديق في خطإ، ولا يمنعنك من اتباع الحق أيضا نسبته إلى أي مجتهد من المجتهدين، فالحق أحق أن يتبع مطلقا، وعلى هذا فالباحث غير المقلد إذا وجد الحق فوجد قوة الدليل وقوة الطرح وتكييف المسألة بوجه واضح لدى الظاهرية أو لدى الزيدية فلا مانع من أن يرجح ذلك المذهب لكن ليس معناه أن يرجحه بسبب انتسابه لأهل البدعة للمذهب الزيدي مثلا أو غير ذلك، ولا يمكن أن يقال إن تآليفهم أحكم وأتقن من تآليف أهل السنة، بل تآليف أهل السنة كما لا يخفى من ما ذكرنا هي أضعاف مضاعفة لكل ما ألفوه حتى لو أخذت كل كتاب للزيدية مثلا قارنته بمائة كتاب من كتب أهل السنة ماذا سيعدل هو في مقابله، وكذلك كتب الظاهرية قارن أي كتاب من كتبهم مثلا اجعل في مقابله ألف كتاب من كتب غيره من المذاهب الأخرى.

سؤال هنا عن أقوال التابعين ومن دونهم من المقطوعات المبثوثة المنتشرة في كتب التفسير وفي غيرها من الكتب عن طريقة الثقة بها ومن أين لنا أن نعرف إسنادها؟

الجواب أن الآثار قد سبق أن ذكرنا في الحديث العناية بها، وأن بعض المؤلفين اعتنوا فقط بالآثار غير المرفوعة إلى النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم، ومن هؤلاء أبو يوسف صاحب أبي حنيفة فله كتاب الآثار، وكذلك محمد بن الحسن الشيباني له كتاب الآثار، وكذلك الطحاوي له شرح معاني الآثار، وكذلك الإمام البيهقي في سننه أورد كثيرا من هذه الآثار، وكذلك عبد الرزاق في مصنفه، وابن أبي شيبة في مصنفه يوردون كل هذه الآثار بأسانيدهم، هذه الأسانيد ينظر فيها مثلما ينظر في أسانيد الأحاديث المرفوعة تماما، فما صح إلى صاحبه صح الإسناد إلى صاحبه ثم بعد ذلك تبقى المناقشة في اجتهاد صاحبه، بينما ما صح إلى النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم لا تبقى مناقشة حينئذ.

ولا شك أن دواوين السنة الأخرى غير خالية من الآثار، فصحيح البخاري فيه عدد كبير من الآثار، صحيح مسلم كذلك فيه عدد دون ذلك، وكتب السنن فيها كثير من الآثار، والموطأ فيه كثير من الآثار، فالآثار دراستها سهلة مثل دراسة الأحاديث المرفوعة تماما، لكن بعض الباحثين المعاصرين بل كثير منهم يعتني بتخريج الأحاديث والحكم عليها أما الآثار فلا يحكم عليها في الغالب، وهذا خطأ منهجي اعتمدته بعض الجامعات الموجودة اليوم، ولكن لا أرى له وجها، من ناحية الصواب ما فيه فرق بينه وبين الأحاديث، كثير من الآثار إذا لم يجدها الإنسان في الكتب التي ذكرنا يمكن أن يرجع إلى كتب التراجم، وفي الكتب التي تعتني بإيراد مرويات الرواة، مثل الكامل لابن عدي، فإنه يعتني بإيراد مرويات كل راو، وكذلك حتى في الإصابة مثلا للحافظ ابن حجر يعتني في بعض الأحيان بالرواية عن كل، وكذلك حتى الذهبي قبله يعتني ببعض الآثار المروية عن بعض المترجمين.

كذلك ابن سعد في كتاب الطبقات يورد كثيرا من الآثار عن كثير من الصحابة والتابعين الذين ترجم لهم، وبعض كتب التفسير أيضا تأتي بالأسانيد في الآثار، مثل كتاب الطبري ومثل كتاب النسائي ومثل كتاب عبد الرحمن بن أبي حاتم الرازي، يوردون الآثار بأسانيدهم إلى أصحابها، وحينئذ لا مشكلة.

أما إذا لم يجد الإنسان إسنادا للأثر بالكلية فليبحث عنه في الكتب الأخرى النادرة الوجود مثل العلل للدارقطني، ومثل العلل لابن أبي حاتم الرازي، ومثل المراسيل لابن أبي حاتم، ومثل المراسيل لأبي داوود، فهذه المراسيل في كثير من الأحيان يقصدون بها آثارا ليست مراسيل بالمصطلح الحديث، إنما يقصدون بها الآثار.

السؤال هنا عن فرق الخوارج الأخرى غير الإباضية هل بقي لها شيء من الكتب، الجواب أن آخر فرق الخوارج غير الإباضية هي الصفرية وقد اندرست في القرن الخامس الهجري ولم يبق لها أثر، أما ما قبل ذلك ففرق الخوارج الأخرى مثل الأزارقة ومثل الطريفية أصحاب الوليد بن طريف ومثل عدد من الفرق الأخرى فقد اندرست ولم يبق لها شيء، أما تأثير الاعتقاد في المؤلفات والمناهج فهو واضح جدا وكبير، ولذلك فإن الشافعي رحمه الله قال في الأم: لا أرد شهادة شاهد من أهل القبلة ولا روايته ـ يقصد في الشهادات، والرواية في الأخبار ليست في الحديث، إذا قال رأى الهلال أو نحو ذلك ـ إلا الخطابية فإنهم يستبيحون الكذب للشهادة لمن وافقهم في نحلتهم، الخطابية وحدهم يرد شهادتهم مطلقا، ولا شك أن الجعفرية المذهب الإمامي يشتهر فيه كثير من الكذب والوضع، ولكن ذلك الوضع يكون من قبل الرؤوس الكبار أما من دونهم فيقدسون تلك الكتب تقديسا كبيرا ولا يستطيعون الجراءة على تغيير أي شيء فيها، أما الخوارج فهم يرون أن الكذب كفر فلذلك يعتنون بالدقة في النقل، ومع هذا لا تخلو كتبهم أيضا من بعض الضعيف والموضوعات، ويعتمدون في كثير من الأحيان على أمور واهية جدا مثل أهل السنة أيضا، فأهل السنة يوجد الاستدلال بالأحاديث الواهية جدا لديهم.

بالنسبة للسؤال هنا عن مذهب الإباضية والزيدية يقال إنهما أقرب مذاهب المبتدعة لأهل السنة؟

بالنسبة للسؤال عن الإمام الشوكاني هل هو مجتهد مطلق أو هو مجتهد تابع؟

الجواب أن تأخر زمانه منعه من رتبة الاجتهاد المطلق، لأنه لم يبق شيء جديد يمكن أن يقوله في مجال أصول الفقه، كل ما يفعله هو تلفيق بين أقوال من سبقوه، ونظير هذا ما ذكرناه من قبل عن شيخ الإسلام ابن تيمية مع البون الشاسع بينهما في الزمان وفي المكانة العلمية وفي غير ذلك، فنحن إذا قلنا إن شيخ الإسلام ابن تيمية لا يصل إلى مرتبة الاجتهاد المطلق فكيف بالشوكاني، القضية أن الاحتمالات الأصولية التي تحتملها العقول قد انتهت، فمجرد التلفيق بينها لا يمكن أن يكون صاحبه مجتهدا مطلقا، لأنه لا بد أن يترجح لديه شيء من كلام من سبقه، تارة بالنظر إلى دليله، وتارة بكثرة القائلين به، وتارة يرجع عن ترجيحه إلى ترجيح الكفة الأخرى وهكذا، ولهذا فالشوكاني رحمه الله أكثر كتبه تلخيصات لكتب السابقين، فكتابه في الأصول إرشاد الفحول كما سنذكر إن شاء الله في كتب الأصول هو تلخيص لكتاب البحر المحيط للزركشي، وكتابه في التفسير هو تلخيص لكتاب القرطبي وكتاب السيوطي جمعهما فيه، الدر المنثور هو تفسير القرطبي وهكذا في كتبه الأخرى، يحاول التلخيص دائما والجمع، ولهذا فهو في الأصول تارة يرجح قولا ثم ينسى أنه رجحه وفي المسألة اللاحقة يرجح ما يبنى على القول الآخر المرجوح عنده في المسألة السابقة، هذا حصل له في عدد من المواضع في إرشاد الفحول.

السؤال هنا عن القول بأن الاجتهاد المطلق ختم بأئمة المذاهب الأربعة هل هو صحيح أو غير صحيح؟

الجواب أنه غير صحيح لأنه جاء بعدهم داوود الظاهري وجاء بعدهم محمد بن جرير الطبري ولا شك أنهما أتيا بأقوال جديدة، لكن المشكلة هنا أن بعض الذين ابتكروا أقوالا في الأصول هم من أتباع المذاهب الذين ما وصلوا في الفقه إلى مرتبة الاجتهاد المطلق ولا في الحديث ولا في التفسير لكنهم ابتكروا في الأصول، وهؤلاء من أمثال أبي بكر الباقلاني في المذهب المالكي، فلا شك أنه مبتكر في الأصول وأتى بأشياء جديدة ليست لدى المالكية من قبل، ومثله الأفري وابن القصار وابن خويز منداد أتوا بأشياء جديدة غير موجودة لدى المالكية من قبل، وكذلك القرافي من المتأخرين والشاطبي بعده، هؤلاء أتوا بأشياء جديدة غير موجودة لدى المالكيين القدماء، لكن لم تكن أهليتهم في العلوم الأخرى تمكنهم من الاجتهاد المطلق فبقوا داخل المذهب، وكذلك في المذاهب الأخرى فمثلا القاضي حسين وأبو المعالي الجويني والغزالي والفخر الرازي والآمدي في المذهب الشافعي لا شك أنهم أتوا بأشياء جديدة في الأصول كثيرة، لكن لم تكن مؤهلاتهم في الأمور الأخرى ترتفع بهم إلى الخروج عن المذهب الشافعي وهكذا، فالقضية هنا قضية التخصصات، الاكتمال صعب، والذين حصل لهم الاكتمال إلى المرتبة التي توصل أصحابها إلى الاجتهاد المطلق كانوا في عصور متأخرة ما كانت الاحتمالات فيها باقية، فلهذا لا شك أن عصر ابن تيمية كان في ذلك الوقت نهضة علمية كبيرة جدا وبالأخص في الشام ومصر، وظهر فيها فطاحلة كبار جدا في علوم مختلفة، وكان هو تتلمذ على عدد منهم فجمع كثيرا من ما لديهم، ففي ذلك الوقت مثلا في الحديث الحافظ المزي لا شك أنه جمع فأوعى وتلامذته كذلك، كذلك الهيثمي لا شك أنه من أجمع الناس في الحديث وأبلغهم اطلاعا عليه، وكذلك في الرجال الحافظ الذهبي آية الدنيا في الرجال، ما له مثل في الإسلام في علم الرجال، وبعد هؤلاء تلامذتهم فمثلا الحافظ زين الدين العراقي في الحديث وقال هو: لقيت عددا من الحفاظ وتركت بعدي حافظين فقط، يقول في آخر عمره لم يبق في الدنيا إلا حافظان: ولدي أبو زرعة ابنه هو الولي ولي الدين وأحمد بن علي بن حجر العسقلاني الحافظ، قال: لم يبق في الدنيا غير هذين الحافظين، ثم جاء بعد ابن حجر عدد من الحفاظ الذين كانت منزلتهم كبيرة مثل الديمي مثل السخاوي ومثل ابن فهد المكي ومثل المحب الطبري ومثل السيوطي هؤلاء الأعلام حفظوا كل شيء، السيوطي كان حفظه في المتون عجيبا جدا، والديمي كان كذلك في الحديث عجيب، والسخاوي في الرجال والعلل.

سؤال: ما سبب انتشار المذهب الحنفي رغم أنه يعتمد على الرأي؟ هل هو مجرد قيام الحكومات عليه ودعمها له؟ أو له قوة ذاتية في نفس المذهب تقتضي ذلك؟

الجواب: أن الاعتماد على الرأي هو ما قلنا من قبل أنه مجرد اصطلاح، وإلا فلا يمكن أن يكون هذا المذهب الكبير الموافق لكثير من الأحاديث الذي أدلته بآلاف الاحاديث الآن مبني على الرأي فقط، ولذلك قال أحد المناظرين من الحنفية هو الإمام العيني عندما ناظره أحد علماء مصر فقال له: إن أبا حنيفة لم يرو إلا ثلاثة عشر حديثا، فقال: هذه مزية لأبي حنيفة ما مثلها مزية، إذا كان أنتج كل هذه المسائل الفقهية الموافقة لحديث النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم وهو لا يعرفه فمعناه أنه موافق للحديث، عمر بن الخطاب وافق الوحي في مسائل قليلة فكانت مزية عظيمة له، فكيف بأبي حنيفة الذي وافقه في آلاف المسائل، آلاف المسائل عند الحنفية موافقة للأحاديث الصحيحة، إذا كان هو لا يعرف الأحاديث وإنما أداه عقله إلى موافقة الوحي هذه مزية عظيمة جدا، وإذا كان يعرفها فكيف تقول هذا الكلام، فإذن القضية ليست على إطلاقها، الحنفية مذهبهم مثل غيره من المذاهب، وأدلتهم لا تخلو عن أن تكون مثل أدلة غيرهم، وإذا رجعت إلى الأحاديث التي عليها مدار الإسلام مثلا أحد عشر ألف حديث في الأحكام، وهذه تتوزعها المذاهب، وليس نصيب مذهب منها أكبر من نصيب مذهب، ولهذا فكل مذهب اعتنى أصحابه بجمع أدلته، وقد ذكرنا أن من أحسن كتب التخريج نصب الراية للحنفية للزيلعي فهو من أحسن كتب التخريج تخريج الأدلة، مع أن المالكية الذين اشتهروا بحفظ الحديث والدراية به تعبوا وتعبوا تعبا شديدا في جمع أدلتهم كتبهم لا تصل إلى مستوى الزيلعي، مثلا كتب الحافظ عبد الحق الإشبيلي الأحكام الكبرى والأحكام الوسطى والأحكام الصغرى، مع تعبه هو وهو حافظ عملاق كان يحفظ مائة ألف حديث بأسانيدها ومتونها يمليها على الناس إملاء ومع هذا كتبه الآن ما لها من الذكر في الإسلام ما لكتاب الزيلعي، مع أن كتبه طار بها الناس في الشرق والغرب، واعتمدت عليها المذاهب كلها، وألف أبو الحسن بن القطان الفاسي كتاب: بيان الوهم والإيهام، تتبع به أخطاء عبد الحق الإشبيلي في الأحكام الوسطى، وهذا الكتاب أيضا من كتب العلل البارزة القوية يعتمد عليه الحافظ ابن حجر مثلا فمن دونه، فعلى هذا القضية نسبية دائما.

بالنسبة لهذه القضية التي يقال إنهم يردون الحديث بالرأي هذه القضية أيضا ليست على إطلاقها ليست كما هي، لا بد أن ينظر الإنسان بتثبت وأن يعرف ما المقصود حينئذ، الحنفية عندهم قواعد عليها كثير من الأدلة المتواترة، وهذه القواعد جعلوها أصولا فحاولوا رد الشريعة كلها إليها، إذن هذه القواعد بثلاثة مكاييل، فإذا وجدوا فرعا شاذا مستثنى يسمونه استحسانا، استثناء من القواعد، ولذلك إذا وجدوا عددا كبيرا من المتواترات في وجه ووجدوا حديثا يخالفه ليس عليه العمل يتركون العمل بالحديث وهذا ليس مختصا بهم بل هذا عند المالكية وعند الحنابلة وعند الشافعية، كثير من نظائره، أما ما ذكر في حديث القلتين، فالحديث أصلا أنا أقتنع بأنه لا يصح عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم لعدة أمور فالحديث مداره على محمد بن إسحاق والوليد بن أبي كثير، محمد بن إسحاق كلام مالك فيه معروف وكلام غيره أيضا، والوليد بن أبي كثير إباضي خارجي، وكلاهما اختلف عليه فيه، فتارة يرويانه عن محمد بن عباد بن جعفر بن الزبير وتارة عن محمد بن جعفر بن الزبير، ثم كل واحد من هذين اختلف عليه فيه فتارة يرويانه عن عبد الله بن عبد الله بن عمر المكبر وتارة عن عبيد الله بن عبد الله بن عمر المصغر، ثم إنه بعد ذلك مضطرب في المتن، فإنه فيه: إذا بلغ الماء قلتين أو ثلاثا في سنن الترمذي، وفيه إذا بلغ الماء مائة قلة وهذا في سنن الدارقطني، وأيضا فإن القلال غير مقدرة، وبالأخص أنها لم يرد في تقديرها إلا ما ذكره البيهقي أنها من قلال هجر، وهذا في الواقع مداره على المغيرة بن صقلاب والمغيرة بن صقلاب ضعيف لدى كل أهل الحديث، فإذن لا اعتبار لهذا التقدير، ثم بعد ذلك فإن الحديث في لفظه أيضا إشكال، الحديث عن ابن عمر أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم سئل عن الماء يكون في الفلاة من الأرض وما ينوبه من السباع والدواب، فقال: إذا بلغ الماء قلتين لم يحمل الخبث، ما معنى لم يحمل، لم يحمل الخبث ما معنى هذه الكلمة، إذن الإشكال موجود على كل حال، ولهذا ترك الحنفية له ليس فقط من باب ترك الحديث بالرأي بل من الناحية الحديثية الصحة أولا ليس صحيحا، ثانيا من ناحية التقدير ما فيه شيء يقدر القلتين، وحتى لو قلنا إن رواية المغيرة بن صقلاب لو وجدت لها متابعة أو شاهد وصححناها فرضا هذا ما لا يمكن، فقلال هجر متفاوتة الأحجام، ولذلك فإن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم شبه بها نبق سدرة المنتهى، قال: فإذا ورقها كآذان الفيلة وإذا نبقها كقلال هجر، ونبق السدرة دائما متفاوت الحجم، فكذلك قلال هجر.

السؤال هنا كيف نصل إلى الراجح في المذهب الحنبلي عند تعدد الروايات؟

الجواب أن هذا هو الذي اشتغل به عدد من الأئمة ومن أهم ذلك كتاب المرداوي الإنصاف، فهو يحاول أن يجمع الروايات ثم يبين لك ما هو المذهب منه، ولدى المتأخرين كذلك زيادات عليه ومتابعات له، لكن كتاب المرداوي من أهم الكتب في هذا الباب.

سؤال عن بعض التوجهات الحديثة في الدراسات التي تعتني بجمع فقه بعض أئمة السلف في مسائل معينة ويجعلونها بهذا العنوان، فقه فلان من الصحابة أو من التابعين أو من أتباعهم؟

سؤال عن أن هذا العمل قد يسهل على الباحث الاطلاع على آراء الصحابة والتابعين هل ذلك صحيح؟

الجواب: نعم إذا كان ذلك في كتب الآثار، إذا كان ذلك في جمع كتب الآثار التي تجمع أقوال عدد من الناس حتى تغطي مساحة كبيرة من الفقه أما إذا كان لمجرد أقوال فلان من الناس ونريد أن نجعل له مذهبا كاملا مثلا نبوب له مثل أبواب الفقه باب الطهارة وما روي عن سعيد فيه، وباب الصلاة، وباب الزكاة وهكذا فهذا غير صحيح، فما لهم من الاجتهادات التي تغطي هذه المساحات، بل إن كثيرا منهم قد يكون المروي عنه في كثير من الكتب الفقهية الكبيرة مسألة أو مسألتان أو نحو ذلك، فهذا حيف عليهم وظلم لهم، ولذلك فإن الذين يشتغلون بهذا النوع من الدراسات سيأخذون عمن هب ودب ويولدون المسائل ويبحثون عن المتردية والنطيحة وما أكل السبع حتى يرقعوا الأبواب الفقهية.

السؤال الثاني عن أن بعض المغرضين إذا نظروا في الفقه فوجدوا الخلافات الكثيرة والردود

t: The Islamic Religious Sciences — Tape Thirteen
a: العلوم الشرعية -الشريط الثالث عشر -
b:
in the name of god, the merciful, the compassionate. praise belongs to god, lord of the worlds, and may god bless our prophet muhammad and his family and all his companions and grant them peace.

among the religious sciences that are objectives in their own right is the science of jurisprudence (fiqh). it is among the noblest and most exalted of the religious sciences, for it is what orders the relations of god's servants with their lord and their relations with one another, and sets out for them the rulings on whatever they have need of. following the same method as with the sciences treated earlier, we begin with the definition of fiqh. its definition falls into two parts: definition in the compound sense (al-maʿnā al-iḍāfī) and definition in the sense of a proper name for a discipline (al-maʿnā al-laqabī).

as for its definition in the compound sense: the expression "the science of fiqh" is a genitive compound whose first term is "science" (ʿilm), which is the verbal noun of ʿalima al-shayʾ — to encompass a thing and grasp it. fiqh in the language means understanding, and from this are the words of god most high: {they said: o shuʿayb, we do not understand much of what you say} (sūrat hūd 11:91) — that is, we do not comprehend it. fiqh as a technical term is knowledge of the practical rulings of the sharia, acquired from their evidences.

a ruling of the sharia (al-ḥukm al-sharʿī) is what comes in the address of god, mighty and majestic, directed to his servants with a view to action. a rational ruling (al-ḥukm al-ʿaqlī) is a proposition — that is, what admits of being true or false — without depending upon revelation or upon custom. a customary ruling (al-ḥukm al-ʿādī) is the affirming of one thing of another, or the denial of it, by way of repeated occurrence, while it remains sound that the pattern should fail — as in the whole of the natural sciences, for the rulings in them are taken only from custom, from repetition, while admitting that the pattern may fail. sharʿ in the language means making manifest, …

sharʿ as a technical term is what god has set out for his servants of the rulings of their religion. it was named sharʿ on account of that setting out, because god made it manifest and clarified it; and also because it is the source they resort to and drink from, as the prophet, may god bless him and grant him peace, made clear by the similitude he struck.

"knowledge of the practical rulings of the sharia": the rulings of the sharia that god has set out for his servants fall into two kinds — rulings of knowledge and rulings of action. those of knowledge are the ones to which no action attaches; the servants simply know them from what god has set out for them, and build their conceptions and their understanding upon them. among these are the matters of creed (ʿaqīdah), for no action attaches to them in themselves, even though they require action. all deeds are required by creed; but creed in itself is not a deed. it is among the works of the heart: it is known, and it does not attach to the limbs. the opposite of that is what attaches to actual deeds — that is, the practical side of the religion — and this is what is meant by fiqh. that is why he said "the practical rulings of the sharia". some of them say instead "the derivative rulings" (al-farʿiyyah), so as to exclude the fundamental ones, which are the rulings of creed. but this goes back to the terminology of the muʿtazilah, for it is they who make the religion into fundamentals (uṣūl) and derivatives (furūʿ). this term of theirs gained currency and invaded the people of the sunnah, and it became well known in the books of the later scholars — even though shaykh al-islam ibn taymiyyah, may god have mercy on him, was among those who did not hold this distinction to be sound. he held that this distinction is in origin taken from the muʿtazilah, and that people built many things upon it: so independent legal reasoning (ijtihād) in creedal matters became blameworthy and was thrown back at those who engaged in it, because people had made those matters fundamentals; and errors in them became greater than errors in other things, and especially in those of them that are open to independent reasoning. this is a mistake. all of it is the religion of god and all of it is alike; all of it is from god. what requires knowledge and what requires action are on the same footing in this. that is why he, may god have mercy on him, said: everyone who exerts himself in seeking the truth is excused, whether he is right or wrong, whether that is in the fundamentals or in the derivatives, because each of them is from god.

something similar to this distinction is the claim that among creedal matters there are fundamentals without which no deed is accepted from a person — as, for example, the six pillars of faith. but the answer to this is that the practical matters are likewise: prayer, zakat and fasting, as pillars of islam. whoever does not pronounce the two testimonies, and does not pray, and does not pay zakat, and does not fast, and does not perform the hajj — from him too this is not accepted. the same applies to the negative matters, that is, the things that are denied: the prohibition of fornication, of wine, of killing the soul that god has forbidden except by right, and the rest of the destructive sins. these are known from the religion by necessity, and whoever denies any of them is not one of the muslims. it is not possible for a person to be counted a muslim unless he knows the necessities of the religion, whether they are matters of knowledge or matters of action. those of knowledge among them are such as the six pillars of faith; those of action are such as the five pillars of islam; and likewise the negative matters that stand in the position of pillars, such as the prohibition of killing a soul, the prohibition of fornication, the prohibition of drinking wine and the prohibition of the flesh of swine. these are the greatest of the things denied in the religion, and it is not possible for a person to be one of the muslims while he does not know that the religion forbids them.

"acquired from their detailed evidences": knowledge of the practical rulings of the sharia is of two kinds. one kind of it is revealed and not acquired, as god revealed it to his messenger, may god bless him and grant him peace, directly. this the prophet, may god bless him and grant him peace, did not acquire, because prophethood is not acquired; rather it is a divine choosing — {he creates what he wills and chooses; they have no choice} (sūrat al-qaṣaṣ 28:68); {god chooses messengers from among the angels and from among men} (sūrat al-ḥajj 22:75). so what was revealed to the prophet, may god bless him and grant him peace, of rulings is not called fiqh, because fiqh means understanding, as though he had produced it; and this he did not produce, because it was revealed to him. it must therefore be acquired: fiqh is applied only to acquired matters. for this reason the points of scholarly consensus (ijmāʿ), in which there are explicit texts of the sharia and the like, are not said to be anyone's school of opinion. one does not say: so-and-so's position is that prayer is obligatory (wājib), or that zakat is obligatory, or that the hajj is obligatory, for example. therefore these matters, even though they are mentioned within fiqh, are not part of fiqh in the technical sense; rather they are part of the religion, part of islam.

"from their detailed evidences": from where is fiqh acquired? there is no doubt that the lawgiver is god, glorified and exalted. he alone is the all-knowing, the all-aware, the one who is informed of the innermost realities of matters and of what they come to, and so he is the one who is able to legislate for his servants. on this basis, there is no legislation except from him. but legislation from him divides into two kinds: clarified legislation (mubayyan) and unelaborated legislation (mujmal). clarified legislation is that in which the details have come; unelaborated legislation is that in which the operative causes recognised by the sharia have been set out, so that we draw an analogy from each case to whatever resembles it. all of this is god's ruling, but it did not come in detail and was not stated by specific designations; rather its legislation came in general terms.

"from their evidences" — and adillah is the plural of dalīl:

*when he alights among the yaḥṣubī, then say to him*

*there will come to rest above me one dark of plumage*

*take provision with you and seek help from a guide* — that is, from the one who shows you the way. "to knowledge": what is meant by it is apprehension in the absolute sense, so that it takes in both certainty and probable opinion, because among the evidences there are those that entail certainty — and this is what the logicians call a dalīl — and among them there are those that lead only to probable opinion, and this is what the logicians call an amārah (an indication).

the evidences of the sharia divide into two kinds: general evidences and detailed evidences. the general evidences are the genera of evidence, such as the book, the sunnah, scholarly consensus, analogical reasoning (qiyās) and inferential reasoning (istidlāl). the detailed evidences are like their parts: every verse of the qur'an from which a ruling is taken is a detailed evidence for that ruling.

this, then, is the limit of the definition of the science when it is taken as a genitive compound. as for the definition of fiqh in the sense of a proper name — that is, as the name of one of the sciences — we can define it by the technical definition of fiqh, except that we add a word to it, so we say: acquaintance with the practical rulings of the sharia from their detailed evidences.

as for the founder of this science, no particular founder can be designated for it, because the prophet, may god bless him and grant him peace — the preponderant of the views of the legal theorists is that he exercised independent reasoning in what no ruling had been sent down to him about, and the matters in which he exercised independent reasoning belong to the domain of fiqh. others, however, raise an objection and say: rather, he was confirmed in them by the sharia, and his being confirmed in them is revelation; and on this basis his exercises of independent reasoning are not counted as fiqh either, but rather as evidences. so the act of the prophet, may god bless him and grant him peace, even if it was by his own independent reasoning, is an evidence and not fiqh.

some people went beyond this until they arrived at holding that every act in his time as well — even if it was from the independent reasoning of the companions — is not counted as fiqh but is rather an evidence, because god most high confirmed them in it. they adduced as evidence the words of jabir, may god be pleased with him: "we used to practise withdrawal while the qur'an was being sent down." this is a confirmation from god; and god's confirmation is more telling than the confirmation of his messenger, may god bless him and grant him peace. the confirmation of the messenger of god, may god bless him and grant him peace, is one category of the evidences, because it is one of the divisions of the sunnah; and god's confirmation likewise, because when an act occurs at the time when the sharia is being sent down and the lawgiver does not forbid it, that indicates that it is permissible (mubāḥ).

as for the independent reasonings of his companions after his death, may god bless him and grant him peace, these belong to fiqh. but given that much of their reasoning was only a working out of detail for what had come in principle in the revelation, and given also that it is little when compared with the reasoning of others, for this reason they did not have an independent body of fiqh. indeed, many people hold that the fiqh of the companions — even by their independent reasonings after the death of the prophet, may god bless him and grant him peace — counts as an evidence and does not count as fiqh, and so they say: the statement of a companion is an evidence without qualification. but among the legal theorists there are those who distinguish and say: the statement of a companion, when it runs contrary to analogy, is an evidence; and his statement in agreement with analogy is not an evidence, because it belongs to fiqh — it is possible that he reasoned to it independently without a transmitted basis. in general, the sphere of fiqh within the practice and the statements of the companions is narrow and small.

but fiqh began from the days of the successors (al-tābiʿūn), and in their days two schools in fiqh became well known. one of them people afterwards called the school of transmitted practice (madrasat al-athar), and the other they called the school of considered opinion (madrasat al-raʾy). the school of transmitted practice was in the hijaz, and the school of considered opinion in iraq. what is meant by athar here is attention to what is transmitted from the predecessors among the companions and the senior successors — that is, giving that precedence over putting the intellect to work and reasoning independently about what newly arises; in other words, attempting to refer every case back to whatever resembles it in the practice of the predecessors, without ranging widely in applying their own minds to the solutions. and what is meant by raʾy, likewise, is putting the intellect to work and ranging widely in that, in what concerns solutions for new questions. on this basis, both schools together have in them a side of considered opinion and a side of transmitted practice: the school of considered opinion is not idle with respect to transmitted practice, and the school of transmitted practice is not idle with respect to considered opinion. this division occurred even in the sciences later on, as we mentioned before in the case of exegesis, for we mentioned that the people of exegesis divided into a school of considered opinion and a school of transmitted practice. but we said that as for the school of transmitted practice, everything it transmits is considered opinion. if it is said to you, "this is one of the commentaries that give attention to transmitted practice," look at it and you will find that most of what it transmits is opinions — either his own opinions, or the opinions of his teachers, or the opinions of the followers of the successors, or the opinions of the successors, or the opinions of the companions. and likewise in the case of considered opinion, its foundation rests upon transmitted practice, because they cannot fall back, in deriving the rulings of the sharia, upon a void or upon the mere approvals of the intellect; rather they fall back in them only upon what is transmitted.

in the days of the successors, the school of transmitted practice turned upon the jurists of medina, who are the famous leading figures among the successors. some restrict them to seven, some make them nine, and some add more; but the important thing is that it is a single school, in agreement. among them are saʿid ibn al-musayyib ibn hazn ibn wahb ibn ʿamr ibn ʿaʾidh ibn ʿimran ibn ʿabd allah ibn makhzum ibn yaqazah ibn murrah al-qurashi; ʿurwah ibn al-zubayr ibn al-ʿawwam ibn khuwaylid ibn asad ibn ʿabd al-ʿuzza ibn qusayy al-qurashi; al-qasim ibn muhammad ibn abi bakr al-siddiq ibn abi quhafah ʿuthman ibn ʿamr ibn kaʿb ibn saʿd ibn taym ibn murrah ibn kaʿb ibn luʾayy ibn ghalib al-qurashi; abu salamah ibn ʿabd al-rahman ibn ʿawf ibn ʿabd ʿawf ibn al-harith ibn zuhrah ibn kilab ibn murrah ibn luʾayy ibn ghalib al-qurashi; ʿubayd allah ibn ʿabd allah ibn ʿutbah ibn masʿud al-hudhali, who is among the confederates of banu zuhrah of quraysh; abu bakr ibn ʿabd al-rahman ibn al-harith ibn hisham al-qurashi likewise; and likewise sulayman ibn yasar al-hilali, of banu ʿamir ibn saʿsaʿah by clientage, for he was a freedman of the mother of the believers maymunah bint al-harith al-hilaliyyah; and likewise abu bakr ibn ʿamr ibn hazm al-ansari; kharijah ibn zayd ibn thabit al-ansari; and salim ibn ʿabd allah ibn ʿumar ibn al-khattab ibn ʿamr ibn nufayl ibn ʿabd al-ʿuzza ibn riyah.

these are approximately the leading successors upon whom the giving of legal opinions in medina turned, and with them others among the jurists of medina who were also successors. in iraq were the people of considered opinion, and among them hammad became well known …

then the learning of the school of transmitted practice passed to abu ʿabd allah malik ibn anas ibn malik ibn abi ʿamir ibn ʿamr ibn al-harith ibn ghayman ibn khuthayl ibn ʿamr ibn al-harith.

of these schools, there remain only those that had followers or partisans, or those upon which states were founded and which governments patronised. the hanafi school enjoyed adoption in the abbasid state when harun al-rashid appointed abu yusuf, the companion of abu hanifah, to the judiciary. he was the first to hold the general judgeship in the islamic state, and was called the chief judge (qāḍī al-quḍāt). likewise when the various states in egypt, the lands of the maghrib and andalusia relied upon the maliki school: sahnun ibn saʿid al-tanukhi, whose name was ʿabd al-salam, was the judge of tunis and qayrawan; ʿabd al-malik ibn habib was the judge of andalusia; and al-bahlul ibn rashid, ʿabd allah ibn farrukh and ʿabd allah ibn ghanim in barqah were a point of reference for the giving of legal opinions and for judgement. these are among malik's companions, except that sahnun and ʿabd al-malik ibn habib did not meet malik; rather they are among the companions of his companions, for they are the students of ʿabd al-rahman ibn al-qasim al-ʿutaqi, of ashhab and of al-harith ibn miskin, who are among malik's companions. likewise the shafiʿi school enjoyed al-mutawakkil ibn al-muʿtasim's taking it up. he is the first caliph of the muslims to affiliate to a school, because it is known that a caliph of the muslims is required to be a practitioner of independent legal reasoning in the religion, and not to be a follower of anyone else, since he is one who is followed and so cannot be a follower. the first of the caliphs of the muslims to follow a school was al-mutawakkil, and he is the tenth of the abbasid caliphs; he followed the shafiʿi school. as for the hanbali school, it had no official standing at the beginning; but for all that, it spread in the lands of palestine, and particularly in nablus and jerusalem, and it continued in them for centuries of time. then some of its scholars were appointed to ministerial office in some states, and that had a resonance which raised the school and helped it to spread.

as for the other schools apart from these four, no followers remained to them and no states were founded upon them — except that certain schools appeared in ages later than these. among them is the school of muhammad ibn jarir al-tabari. he was the leading figure of the people of exegesis and one of the leading figures of the people of hadith, and it has also been mentioned earlier that he is one of the leading figures of the people of historical reports and history. he had followers and partisans in baghdad, and baghdad at that time was the capital of society, the capital of the islamic state. but in view of the disputes that arose between him and the hanbalis, and their pressing hard upon him, his school did not spread, and his school became one of the extinct schools. indeed, some of his books were destroyed in some of the strife that went on between him and them, and among them were some of his books on hadith. likewise dawud ibn ʿali al-zahiri: he had followers in iraq, then his school spread until it reached andalusia. he had followers there, among them al-mundhir ibn saʿid al-ballūṭī, upon whom the umayyad state in andalusia relied; and his school was afterwards championed in andalusia by abu muhammad ʿali ibn hazm al-zahiri. with this, the juristic schools recognised among the people of the sunnah were confined to the hanafi school, the maliki school, the shafiʿi school and the hanbali school, in addition to the remnants of the zahiri school.

as for those apart from them, the shia had a number of juristic schools, but they go back to two great schools, one of them the school of the jaʿfariyyah and the second the school of the zaydiyyah. the jaʿfariyyah are those who affiliate to jaʿfar ibn muhammad al-baqir ibn ʿali zayn al-ʿabidin ibn al-husayn ibn ʿali ibn abi talib, may god be pleased with them all — even though a great number of the factions of the shia, all of them, affiliate to jaʿfar; for everyone apart from those who affiliate to zayd ibn muhammad affiliates to his brother jaʿfar. the shia did not differ over affiliating to muhammad ibn ʿali al-baqir: all their factions go back to him. they differed only over his sons. a number of them went out with zayd, and so they became known as the zaydiyyah; and those who remained and held fast to the school of his brother rejected him, and so were named the rawafid — they are the ones who rejected zayd. the shia, then, are of two kinds: zaydiyyah and rawafid. the zaydiyyah have several juristic schools, and in their school are a number of practitioners of independent legal reasoning; and likewise the rafidi jaʿfariyyah have several schools, in which are a number of practitioners of independent legal reasoning. as for the khawarij, nothing of their schools has remained worth mentioning except the ibadi school, which is the school of the followers of ʿabd allah ibn ibad al-tamimi al-khariji, who was in origin among the followers of nafiʿ ibn al-azraq, of the azariqah of the haruriyyah. so all these schools that have remained to our time and to which there are people today who hold fast are eight schools: the four followed schools of the people of the sunnah, the zahiriyyah, the zaydiyyah, the jaʿfariyyah and the ibadiyyah. these schools likewise differ in the construction of some of the principles to which recourse is had in the details of fiqh.

so, for example, these schools differ over what is to be done when texts conflict: do we begin with reconciling them (jamʿ) or with giving one of them preponderance (tarjīḥ)? they differ likewise over whether the qur'an can be abrogated by the sunnah or cannot be abrogated by it, and whether the qur'an likewise can abrogate the sunnah or cannot abrogate it. they differ likewise over the indication of a general expression (ʿāmm) with respect to the individuals falling under it: is it definitive or probable? if a specific (khāṣṣ) evidence opposes it, is the specific given precedence over it or not? they differ likewise over the indication of an unqualified command: is it obligation (ījāb), or recommendation (nadb), or permissibility (ibāḥah)? they differ likewise over the indication of an unqualified command from the standpoint of legal effect: does it indicate validity or does it not indicate it? and likewise over whether an unqualified command indicates repetition, or indicates immediacy. all of that is among the principles over which disagreement has arisen, and upon the basis of which the schools mentioned were established.

in general, the disagreements among all these schools are in matters open to independent legal reasoning; it is not possible to judge any one of them to be absolutely the most correct. this holds even if the schools have other deviations outside fiqh — even if we were to say, for example, that the rawafid have a deviant creedal school, that does not prevent us from knowing that they have a juristic school with bases that cannot be denied. so on this juristic side, which is built upon understanding the texts and the rules for applying them to particular cases, a plurality of points of view is admissible in it; there is no objection in it to plurality, and correctness in it cannot be claimed to be confined to a single statement or to a single one of the schools. that is hateful partisanship. monopolising the truth in matters open to independent legal reasoning that go back to the intellect is unattainable, because there is no one who puts his mind to work but that his mind will bring him to a point of view which ought to be respected as his, so long as no revealed text bars it and it does not collide with the minds of others.

these schools are likewise not free of schools within them, and of disputes and disagreements inside them. among the companions of abu hanifah, the imam abu yusuf yaʿqub became well known, and he differed from abu hanifah in many matters; and likewise muhammad ibn al-hasan al-shaybani, who differed from abu hanifah and from abu yusuf as well in many questions; and likewise the imam zufar, the third of abu hanifah's companions; and likewise al-hasan ibn salih al-luʾluʾi, the fourth of abu hanifah's companions.

*indeed al-hidāyah, like the qur'an, has abrogated what came before it; so preserve its benefits and master its rules.*

it was served with the most thorough service, and a very great number of commentaries were composed upon it. among its commentaries, for example, is fatḥ al-qadīr by al-kamal ibn al-humam, who is among the eminent verifying scholars of the hanafis; and likewise al-bināyah ʿalā al-hidāyah by al-ʿayni, the commentator on ṣaḥīḥ al-bukhārī; and likewise al-ʿināyah by al-babarti and al-kifāyah by al-baldi, and a great number of other books that revolve in the orbit of al-hidāyah. its hadiths were documented by al-zaylaʿi the elder in his book naṣb al-rāyah fī takhrīj aḥādīth al-hidāyah, which is the first book specialising in the field of documenting hadiths; and al-hafiz ibn hajar abridged it in his book al-dirāyah fī takhrīj aḥādīth al-hidāyah. then after this came al-quduri, and he composed his abridgement, which the hanafis call "the book". it too became the mainstay of the school and the people's point of reference, because he abridged the books of muhammad ibn al-hasan, and particularly because he combined al-jāmiʿ al-kabīr and al-jāmiʿ al-ṣaghīr. so this book became famous, people circulated it and took it up with commentaries; its commentaries became many and it became their mainstay. then came al-nasafi, who is one of their great leading scholars, and he composed his book kanz al-daqāʾiq, and they turned to it as well with great eagerness. among the commentaries on kanz al-daqāʾiq is tabyīn al-ḥaqāʾiq by al-zaylaʿi the younger, the student of the author of naṣb al-rāyah; and among them likewise al-baḥr al-rāʾiq by ibn nujaym, upon which there is ibn ʿabidin's gloss entitled minḥat al-khāliq ʿalā al-baḥr al-rāʾiq ʿalā kanz al-daqāʾiq. and upon tabyīn al-ḥaqāʾiq likewise there is the gloss of ibrahim al-shalabi al-turki. then came the later scholars among them, and they produced many specialised abridgements, among the most famous of which is tanwīr al-abṣār by al-haskafi …

as for the maliki school, the earliest and most important of its books in origin is al-mudawwanah. it is a book that passed from hand to hand and was taken up, for asad ibn al-furat, who was among malik's companions, cast fiqh in the form of questions. so he went and put them to the people of iraq. it is said that he put them at first to malik, who declined to answer him and said: "go to the people of iraq, for my opinions …"

then asad ibn al-furat went to qayrawan and presented the book to them, and they were delighted with it. sahnun asked him to lend it to him so that he might write it out, and he said: "there is no way to that." he negotiated with him until he agreed to lend it to him for a single night. so sahnun distributed it that night among his students and they all wrote it out, so that it came to be written down with them on the sheets. and asad ibn al-furat went to sicily and conquered it, and he was the commander of the army there.

*and it was a light matter to the chiefs of banu luʾayy* — and this line has become a byword, as the poet said:

*i have become a stranger among them, in their very midst* …

this book became famous, and people circulated it and passed it on, and it was transmitted as the mother-books are transmitted — so much so that when the people of toledo were assailed by the spaniards, who burned their books and threw them into the river, there was among their jurists a jurist who knew al-mudawwanah by heart, and he dictated it to them; so a copy of it came to them and they found it just as it had been.

a number of authors abridged it and commented upon it, and it was served with many kinds of service: works were composed on its technical terms, on the rare words of its language, on the documentation of its hadiths and on other matters. among the most famous of those who served it is abu muhammad ʿabd allah ibn abi zayd al-qayrawani, for he composed his book al-nawādir wa-l-ziyādāt in service of al-mudawwanah. then after him the judge abu al-walid muhammad ibn ahmad ibn rushd the elder, the grandfather, and he commented upon its chapter-headings and its sections …

a number of malik's companions composed other books, among the most famous of which are the abridgements of ʿabd allah ibn ʿabd al-hakam, which are the earliest abridgement composed by a muslim.

and likewise the books of ibn wahb, although they did not receive sufficient transmission, because the man was famous for hadith and people were more desirous of his hadith than of his books of fiqh. then after these came muhammad ibn al-mawwaz and muhammad ibn sahnun, who became known as "the two muhammads". ibn al-mawwaz composed al-mawwāziyyah, which is among the most famous and most important of the books of the malikis, and muhammad ibn sahnun composed a great number of books. then the maliki school came to consist of several schools, which can be reduced to about five. the madinan school — this one was not destined to last long, because the shia came to dominate medina afterwards and changed its features and expelled the people of the sunnah from it. the fiqh of this school turns upon the transmission of ʿabd al-malik ibn al-majishun from malik, and upon the transmission of al-mughirah and mutarrif from him. these are the famous madinan companions of malik: ʿabd al-malik ibn al-majishun, mutarrif and al-mughirah.

and the egyptian school, whose pillar is ibn al-qasim, and of which are ashhab, ibn ʿabd al-hakam, ibn nafiʿ and ibn wahb, and their followers after them. and the iraqi school, among the most famous of whose leading figures among malik's companions is the judge ismaʿil, who is of the descendants of hammad ibn zayd and is the author of the book al-mabsūṭ in maliki fiqh; and among the most famous of malik's students in it also is abu musʿab al-zuhri, who was a teacher of the imam ahmad, and likewise yahya ibn yahya al-tamimi and yahya ibn ʿabd allah ibn bukayr. among the later scholars, this school turns upon abu bakr al-abhari, ibn al-qassar and ibn khuwayz mindad — which is also pronounced khuwayz bindad — and the judge ʿabd al-wahhab ibn nasr al-baghdadi. among its most famous books are ʿuyūn al-adillah by ibn al-qassar and his ruʾūs al-masāʾil as well, and the books of the judge ʿabd al-wahhab, among the most famous of which are al-maʿūnah, al-talqīn and his commentary on al-risālah.

then the qayrawani-maghribi school, whose mainstay is sahnun and his students. it is the weightiest and most important of these schools, because it inherited the egyptian school, and in it the school settled for long centuries. then the andalusian school, whose mainstay in origin is yahya ibn yahya al-laythi al-masmudi and ʿabd al-malik ibn habib; and this school was strengthened by the famous leading scholars who became well known in andalusia, such as abu ʿumar yusuf ibn ʿabd allah ibn ʿabd al-barr, the ḥāfiẓ of the maghrib; abu al-walid sulayman ibn khalaf al-baji; and abu al-walid muhammad ibn ahmad ibn rushd the grandfather, and likewise his grandson.

as for the books that gather the views of these schools and are considered a point of reference for the school afterwards, among the earliest of them is the book al-tafrīʿ by ibn al-jallab; then the book of ibn shaʾs — or ibn shas, with the hamzah or without it: shaʾs is one of the well-known arab proper names, and easing the hamzah is permissible in it, so one says shaʾs and shas. then the abridgement of ibn al-hajib, which he named jāmiʿ al-ummahāt. god set acceptance upon the abridgement of ibn al-hajib, and it was served magnificently; eighteen commentaries upon it became well known, among them al-tawḍīḥ by khalil ibn ishaq ibn musa al-jundi, the commentary of ibn ʿabd al-salam al-tunisi, the commentary of ibn harun al-tunisi likewise, the commentary of ibn rashid al-qafsi — and qafsah is a town of tunisia as well — and other commentaries besides. and the book al-mustakhrajah by muhammad ibn al-ʿutbi, in which he gathered the transmissions from malik by other than the route of al-mudawwanah, upon the method of the people of hadith in extraction. this book became so famous that it was a rival to al-mudawwanah — as the imam ibn rushd says in his urging people to attend the sessions of the people of learning and of the judiciary. he says: when i was appointed to the judgeship, the first question was put to me and i did not know what to say about it, and i at that time knew al-mudawwanah and al-mustakhrajah by heart with an exact memorisation. were it not for the counsel of abu saʿid ibn ludd, who had been a judge and a muftī before him — had it not been for his previous practice of attending the sessions of the judiciary, he would not have known how to give judgement, even though he knew al-mudawwanah and al-ʿutbiyyah by heart with an exact memorisation. and abu al-walid ibn rushd the elder composed al-bayān wa-l-taḥṣīl as a commentary upon al-ʿutbiyyah — a commentary upon this al-mustakhrajah — and in it he served it magnificently. and likewise among the mother-books of the malikis is al-jāmiʿ by ibn yunus al-siqilli, in which he attempted to gather the evidences of the malikis, so that many students of knowledge used to call it "the muṣḥaf of the school", because of its gathering of the evidences from the verses and the hadiths — from every verse he extracts many evidences …

and the books of the imam al-maziri, among the most important of which is his commentary on al-talqīn of the judge ʿabd al-wahhab. and al-risālah by abu muhammad ʿabd allah ibn abi zayd al-qayrawani, upon which god set a magnificent acceptance, so that its commentaries are now more than three hundred commentaries, and centuries have passed in which every year a commentary upon it appeared — centuries, every year a new commentary appearing for it. among the most famous of its commentaries today are the commentary of the learned ahmad zarruq al-burnusi and the commentary of ibn naji, both of them printed in a single volume, and the commentary of abu al-hasan …

then came khalil ibn ishaq ibn musa al-jundi al-maliki, and he composed his comprehensive abridgement, in which he was granted a wonderful kind of concision. he gathered into it nearly all these preceding books; in it are one hundred and twenty thousand juristic questions. ibn al-qayyim, may god have mercy on him, said of it: god's kindnesses to the malikis did not cease to follow one upon another until he brought out for them a young man who gathered their school for them into sheets that a man tucks under his arm and walks out with — "tucks under his arm" meaning that he puts them under his armpit and goes out. it is the mainstay of the school today; people memorise it as they memorise the qur'an. it was served with all the kinds of service, and there are more than eighty commentaries upon it, among the most famous of which is the commentary of bahra… and it was presented to the notables at tilimsan.

*he passed over it with his finger in two days, and said, there is no fault in it for one who desires it; i said, from its root it possessed that loftiness* …

and among them is the versification of shaykh muhammad salim; and this versification gathers the rare words of the language as well:

*and upon whom there is a shanq that has melted upon al-sabāhil, fa-ash…*

and so on. he brings in difficult expressions; even the expressions of the rare views in exegesis he brings in as well, so as to tie the reader to the books of exegesis. so, for example, in the chapter on menstruation he says:

*blood that flowed of itself from the sh…*

he brings in the word al-shukr, and the word al-iʿṣār — aʿṣarat means she menstruated — and the word al-ikbār as well, from akbarat. and this ties the reader to the books of exegesis.

the question here is about the muftī: when he is asked for a legal opinion, what is incumbent upon him?

i say that people have three approaches in that. the first approach: if the questioner is one of the people of learning, then it is for the muftī to set out for him the views there are on the question and the evidences for each view, and then to leave the weighing to the one seeking the opinion. and if he is not one of the people of learning who are capable of deriving rulings, he sets it out for him and then weighs for him the view that he holds to be preponderant. this approach is the scholarly approach to giving legal opinions, because it makes the one seeking the opinion not become rigidly confined; for if he sees that one of the schools is more fitting for him and that its evidence is stronger, he is able to take it, and he comes to know which of the questions are matters of disagreement and which of them are not. the second approach is that he gives him the opinion according to the requirement of his own school; for the muftī and the one seeking the opinion are both of them, in most cases

the third approach is that he sets out for him only what the muftī has found preponderant, and gives him a ready-made ruling according to what he alone finds preponderant. and this approach is called …

here is a question about affiliating to a school (tamadhhub) in the first place, and about its ruling, and about the fact that many people call for abandoning school affiliation and say that the scholars who founded the schools took from the book and the sunnah, so why should not all people go back to them?

the answer is that this idea is unattainable and unworkable in the time of the later generations, because the book and the sunnah do not cover all the questions explicitly — all the incidents and novel cases that newly arise, explicitly. the area covered by revelation, of the acts of the legally accountable person and of the one exercising independent legal reasoning, is very small: it does not reach 10% of the acts of the accountable person. the rest of the acts of the accountable are covered only by independent legal reasoning and derivation. and independent legal reasoning and derivation are, without doubt, not restricted to the people of one time nor to the people of one place. but the rules by which the texts are dealt with are limited by reason, so it is not possible that a man should come today — even if he reached the rank of the predecessors in learning — and say: "i shall bring a new view on the indication of the general expression, or on the indication of the unqualified, or on the weighing of evidence." he cannot bring anything, because all the rational possibilities have been exhausted by the predecessors; all that is possible is combining (talfīq), and this is what has remained for the later generations.

and in combining there is no objection: that he should take from this school a given rule and from that one a given rule. but in most cases he will not depart, in the rational matters, from what they have exhausted; and in what is rationally exhausted no renewal can occur. and the schools are not outside the book and the sunnah; rather they only cover the area that is not covered by revelation, because what is covered by revelation, as we mentioned, does not enter into the definition of fiqh at all. fiqh is only those matters in which there is no text and which are rather the independent reasonings of men; and these, of necessity, must give rise to schools. but none of those schools is compulsory upon any person. rather, if a person is a student of knowledge, it is for him to choose from among them the preponderant view, because acting upon the preponderant is obligatory (wājib), not merely preponderant. he searches for what he himself finds preponderant, and he knows that its being preponderant for him does not require that it be preponderant for all people.

for the mere fact that a view is found preponderant by you adds to the supporters of that view by one voice; and over against that, you may find that the other views have many other voices.

likewise, if a person is not fit for this stage and is not a student of knowledge at all, then these schools are a breadth that delivers him — as al-shaʿrani said. he said: the sharia has two walls, one of them the wall of the standing ruling (ʿazīmah) and the second the wall of dispensation (rukhṣah), and all the schools are between these two walls. so if you find a school that is strict in a question, know that it has drawn close to the wall of the standing ruling; and if you find a school that is lenient in it, know that it has drawn close to the wall of dispensation. and look at yourself: are you among those who take dispensations, or among the people of standing rulings? if you are excused by some excuse, or a person of weakness, then go with those who went to the dispensation; and if you are a person of strength and of well-being, then go to those who went to the standing ruling.
